#4463. 10,000 Miles with Our 2026 Mercedes-Benz E450, and the Love Bombing Continues

We can’t get enough of the way the E-class drives.

If you were friends with our long-term Mercedes-Benz E450, and it was in a relationship with someone like us, you’d be no doubt cautioning your friend about our love bombing. The logbook is stuffed, page after page, with over-the-top praise. Here’s a smattering of some recent musings: “Arguably the most comfortable long-termer we’ve ever had,” says managing news editor Eric Stafford. Senior news editor Caleb Miller added, “The E450 just feels so effortless and relaxing that I feel like I could drive across the country in one day in this thing.” And Miller also gave a shoutout to the 21-speaker Burmester sound system. Editor-in-chief Tony Quiroga, who is known to sign out the E-class for extended chunks of time, adds, “Makes you feel so relaxed when you drive it—supple ride, glorious seats, rich interior, plus summer-tire grip.” But Buyer’s Guide director Rich Ceppos may have bestowed the highest praise: “Of the 500-plus models we cover, if I had to pick one car to live with and drive every day, it’d be this one.”

See all results for new 2026 Mercedes-Benz E-class for sale near 60089

It’s safe to say we’re smitten with the way the E-class drives, an ideal blend of comfort and liveliness. If we had one nit to pick it would be the slight impact harshness from the 20-inch wheels and tires and their relatively shallow sidewalls. We’d probably like the ride better with the base 18-inch wheel-and-tire package and its additional sidewall, although it’s a major visual downgrade.

The E450 drives so well, and its 375-hp turbo inline-six is so smooth and melodious, that we’d be more than willing to overlook so-so fuel economy. But the E-class continues to impress there, too, with an overall average of 27 mpg, one better than its EPA combined figure. And that’s with a lot of heavy-footed commuting and not all that many road trips. On longer drives, we’ve seen mpg numbers in the high 30s.

Fall’s cooler temperatures have us in a warm glow about the E450’s not only heated steering wheel and seats (both pretty common nowadays) but also the heated center and outboard armrests, part of the $2950 Multicontour Seating package—decadent, perhaps, but a lovely way to start your commute on a chilly morning.

Our primary complaints tend to be about anything but the driving, including the touch-sensitive controls on the steering wheel, the door handles that sometimes don’t power out of the body quick enough, or the fingerprint-prone piano-black interior trim and vast array of three screens across the interior. We’ve also gotten plenty cross with the virtual assistant, which chimes in with obnoxious frequency if left to its automatic setting, interrupting conversations about everything from building developments in the area to the price of an item discussed. We quickly switched it back to having to hear the “Hey, Mercedes” wake phrase before inserting itself.

See all results for new 2026 Mercedes-Benz E-class for sale near 60089

You know the honeymoon phase is waning when it comes time to start paying for maintenance. Mercedes specifies service for the E-class every 10,000 miles or 12 months, with the first one a simple oil change and various inspections. We felt the Mercedes markup paying that $478 bill, and our local dealer added another $62 of oil and fuel additives that aren’t called for in the owner’s manual and without asking our approval (we’ve excluded this charge from the service-cost tally).

The only other pause in the enjoyment of our E450 was when a screw found its way into the right-front tire in a spot where it couldn’t be plugged. So, we had to shell out $420 for a new tire from Tire Rack, which was there the next day.

Can the love last? We have another 30,000 miles to find out.

Months in Fleet: 5 months Current Mileage: 11,134 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 27 mpgFuel Tank Size: 17.4 gal Observed Fuel Range: 460 milesService: $478 Normal Wear: $0 Repair: $0Damage and Destruction: $420

Ever since this long-term 2026 Mercedes-Benz E450 arrived, it has served us daily reminders why we named this excellent luxury sedan to our 10Best list for two years running. Some of that luxury comes from the fact that we could not drive the car in any other way, because it showed up with a mere 20 miles on its odometer and we were driving gently to follow the 1000-mile break-in requirements. Either way, its ride refinement and all-around sophistication have received continuous accolades since day one. Everyone in the office is already gushing over the E-class's ride quality, refinement, and seat comfort.

Of course, once we hit the 1000-mile mark, we picked up the pace. The around-town ride feels almost floaty, so you'd think that hurling it down a back road would take the E450 out of its element, but it remains tied down and settled no matter how hard you push. Skidpad grip of 0.92 g is excellent for the class, as is braking from 70 mph in 157 feet, which is an identical result to the last BMW M5 we tested.

The E450's inline-six, which pairs exclusively with all-wheel drive and is a $5900 upgrade over the four-cylinder-powered E350, is not only smooth and sonorous, but also extraordinarily fuel efficient. We measured a whopping 39 mpg in our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, which is 6 mpg better than its EPA highway figure. Combined with a decently sized 17.4-gallon fuel tank, that means our E-class can make it nearly 700 miles on a single fill-up. The E450 returns excellent fuel economy beyond purposefully gentle driving too; our current running average of 27 mpg is 1 mpg higher than its EPA combined rating. Considering the straight-line hustle the 375-hp six commands—60 mph in a brisk 4.5 seconds and the quarter-mile in 12.9 seconds—that fuel economy is seriously impressive.

But the steering wheel's touch-sensitive controls are despised as much as the car's overall driving demeanor is loved. Everything from the volume control to the cruise set speed requires a swipe on the steering-wheel spokes, which sometimes does nothing, sometimes provides more adjustment than you're looking for, and rarely does exactly what you want.

Our long-term E450 is packed full of options, taking the price up to $95,375 from its $73,650 starting point. There are a few things that the majority of us could do without, including the front passenger screen and selfie camera (part of the $1500 Superscreen package) and the $990 3-D gauge cluster display. But the $3400 Pinnacle trim, which includes a thumpin' 21-speaker Burmester stereo, and the $3200 air springs that bolster ride quality are outlays that we'd spend our own money on. We also thought ahead to winter; tucked into the various option packages are heaters for the front armrests, steering wheel, rear seats, and washer nozzles. There's really only one feature that we wish we had, and that's soft-close doors, which cost an additional $550. We're fans of the Verde Silver Metallic green paint, and the $1950 20-inch AMG multi-spoke wheels are a serious visual upgrade over the base 18s.

The E-class is not at all ostentatious, but it still gets noticed, with many a parking-lot bystander lobbing praise in the E-class's direction. We agree, it's a fantastic luxury sedan, and we look forward to spending a lot more time driving it to see if we're as smitten with the ownership experience.

#4462. The electric Vespa just got better where it actually matters

Vespa’s electric scooters have never exactly screamed for attention. That’s sort of the point. They look like Vespas, ride like Vespas, and just happen to swap the gasoline engine for a much quieter electric drivetrain.

But for 2027, Vespa has given its electric lineup a fairly significant technological overhaul while leaving that iconic steel bodywork largely untouched.

Unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the new electric Vespa lineup now consists of the Primavera Elettrica, Sprint S Elettrica, and the faster Primavera Tech Elettrica. And while you’d be forgiven for struggling to spot the differences from across the show floor, there’s a lot more happening underneath.

The biggest upgrade is an entirely new electric motor developed and manufactured in Italy by Vespa parent company Piaggio Group. The motor uses a new modular design intended to improve both performance and efficiency, while also doing away with rare-earth materials.

On the 45 km/h (28 mph) Primavera and Sprint S models, Vespa says the new motor provides stronger acceleration for stop-and-go city riding. Range reaches up to 85 km (53 miles) in Eco mode.

But perhaps the biggest practical improvement is the new removable battery. Being able to pull the battery out of the scooter and carry it inside for charging makes a massive difference for urban riders who don’t have access to a garage or dedicated charging spot – exactly the kind of riders Vespa is targeting.

The Primavera Tech is where things get a little faster. This version is homologated as a motorcycle rather than a moped in Europe and reaches 67 km/h (42 mph). That’s still not terribly fast, but the electric Vespa line has never been known for its top speed.

Its range has increased by 12.5% thanks to the new motor and Vehicle Management System, reaching 90 km (56 miles) on the WMTC cycle or up to 100 km (62 miles) in Eco mode.

There’s also a new charger that Vespa says reduces energy consumption from the wall by 17%, with a 0-80% charge taking around 2.5 hours. A new Maintenance mode is designed to protect the battery during longer periods when the scooter isn’t being ridden.

Nice. I've always liked the idea of Vespas. My riding requires something a bit bigger, but they're cute as a button.

The Primavera Tech also gets the technological bells and whistles you’d expect from the flagship version, including a 5-inch TFT display, keyless operation, navigation through Vespa’s smartphone connectivity system, and remote seat unlocking.

Perhaps the most Vespa thing about the whole update is how little of it you can actually see.

The company hasn’t tried to turn its electric scooters into rolling science-fiction props. They’re still unmistakably Vespas, complete with the same classic styling that has defined the brand for generations. They just happen to have a much more interesting electric drivetrain hiding underneath now.

Of course, they also carry some very Vespa pricing. While we don’t have word on the updated pricing for the new models, the outgoing Primavera Elettrica 70 RED was priced at $8,299 in the US. So don’t expect these models to come cheap.

#4461. Cadillac Is Bringing GM’s Super Cruise Hands-Free Driving System To Europe

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Super Cruise, General Motors’ hands-free driving assistance system, is heading to Europe, where it will be available starting in mid-December on a handful of Cadillac EVs.

The 2025 Optiq, as well as the 2026 Lyriq and Vistiq electric crossovers, will be able to do semi-automated driving on more than 180,000 kilometers (111,000 miles) of compatible roads across 16 European countries beginning at the end of the year. Germany, France, and Switzerland are among the first European countries where the system will go live.

Super Cruise, which is already available in the United States, Canada, China, and South Korea, uses pre-mapped roads, real-time cameras, radar sensors, GPS data, and adaptive cruise control to enable hands-free driving. That said, the system is still considered a Level 2 driver assistant, according to the Society of Automotive Engineers, so it doesn’t make the car run autonomously, and the driver still needs to pay attention at all times when driving.

A driver monitoring system makes sure that the person behind the steering wheel is alert and can take control at any time, if needed.

When active, Super Cruise displays a green light bar at the top of the steering wheel. The system keeps the vehicle centered in the lane and maintains an appropriate distance from the car in front, without the driver having to touch the steering wheel or pedals. It can do lane changes, but the driver has to initiate the maneuver by activating the indicator.

The feature can be used on compatible roads, including highways and dual carriageways, at speeds of up to 130 kilometers per hour (81 miles per hour), including in heavy stop-and-go traffic.

Cadillac has integrated Google Maps into the navigation map display, which shows roads where Super Cruise can be used and how much of a trip can be driven hands-free. The automaker says the driver assistance feature is designed to make driving more comfortable and convenient—so drivers shouldn’t expect to be able to take a nap while on the road.

“Super Cruise brings together Cadillac’s premium driving experience, connected services and advanced driver assistance technology to make everyday journeys more comfortable,” said Maximilian Wittich, Managing Director, Digital Services and Experiences. “We are excited to bring this hands-free experience to customers in Europe and to offer technology that has been tested and adapted for European roads and requirements.”

GM said it did a lot of performance testing and validation, as well as regional route testing and Europe-specific software tweaks to make Super Cruise compatible with European legislation and driving conditions.

Since debuting in 2017, Super Cruise has delivered over a billion hands-free driving miles, GM said. In North America alone, there are roughly 750,000 Super Cruise-enabled vehicles, but the American auto giant estimates that the number of users will exceed 850,000 by the end of the year.

In the U.S., over 20 GM models are compatible with Super Cruise. The system is included for free for the first three years from the date of first registration. When the free trial ends, owners need to pay for a Super Cruise subscription and a Connected Services plan to keep using hands-free driving.

#4460. Ford Teases New Mustang Cobra for 2027, Potential Return Of the Flat-Plane Crank V-8

Could the Shelby GT350’s Voodoo engine be coming back with more displacement?

It’s time to get excited, folks. Ford just released an audio clip as a teaser for a new Mustang, and it sure sounds like it could be equipped with a flat-plane crank V-8.

The teaser suggests this new Mustang is to be called Cobra—but it seems more than likely to us that it’ll actually boast the Cobra R name, on account of the “R” being highlighted in blue after Ford spells out “Cobra” in the video. Of course, Ford has some serious history with the Cobra R name, with its last appearance being in the mighty-special 2000 SVT Cobra R.

As for the sound in the video, listen above and make up your own mind, but it sure sounds Voodoo-esque to us. That said, it’s not a dead wringer for the 5.2-liter naturally aspirated flat-plane crank in the old Shelby GT350. What could account for the change? Our best guess is more displacement: if Ford is borrowing the Cobra R name, it would stand to reason that it would also borrow the 5.4 liters of displacement that car had. This would not only honor the past, but substantially move the game forward from where the GT350 left off.

This line of thinking follows a report from yesterday that suggested Ford is cooking up a GT350 successor with power output in the 600-horsepower range and a naturally aspirated V-8. And just like the GT350, this new muscle car is supposedly going to be manual-only. Listening to the audio clip, the vehicle accelerating and revving to the moon is clearly shifted via a manual transmission.

Ford confirms in its text for the teaser that this Mustang is for the purists. “You’ll want to hear this. For the drivers, with an all-motor heart born from racing. Ford Mustang Cobra, a Legacy Reborn. The story continues in 2027.”

If that doesn’t get you a little giddy for the next chapter of the S650-gen Mustang, we’re not sure what would. Ford doesn’t supply a reveal date, but it suggests we’ll get to learn more next year. With 2026 being the year of the Dark Horse SC, it stands to reason that 2027 will be the year of the Cobra R.

#4457. Hyundai Is Recalling Nearly 30,000 Kona EVs Because Their Airbags May Not Deploy

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Hyundai is recalling nearly 30,000 first-generation Kona Electric crossovers in the United States because their airbags and seatbelt pretensioners may not work as intended in the event of an accident.

All affected vehicles, 29,058 in total, were built in South Korea between August 28, 2018, and July 26, 2023, representing model years 2019 through 2023. The problem also affects nearly 9,000 Hyundai Veloster N gas-powered hatchbacks sold here between 2019 and 2022.

The Airbag Control Unit (ACU) is the culprit here. According to the recall report published by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), data that needs to be written to the ACU’s memory may become corrupted during certain driving conditions, causing the airbag malfunction light (MIL) to pop up on the instrument cluster and the airbag system to deactivate.

Without a working system, the airbags will not deploy during a crash, which increases the risk of injury to the driver and passengers.

Hyundai said that the ACU data may become corrupted if a system reboot or a power interruption occurs while the control unit is writing data to its internal memory. The company’s North America office opened a new investigation back in 2024, after the number of airbag warning light warranty claims went up.

The automaker worked with ZF, the supplier that made the airbag control units, to replicate the problem on other vehicles, but couldn’t. However, a fault was induced during bench testing, and a solution was found.

To fix the problem, owners of affected vehicles need to book an appointment with a Hyundai service center, where technicians will update the ACU software for free. In other words, it’s not a hardware fix, but a software fix. According to Hyundai, the new software rolls back to the last known valid data if the transfer is interrupted for one of the reasons described above.

The maker of the Kona EV said that it’s aware of 331 individual incidents related to the ACU issue that affects the electric crossover and gas-powered hot hatch. The car manufacturer is not aware of any crashes, fires, or injuries associated with the ACU data corruption problem in the U.S.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Nissan has offered hybrid versions of the Rogue, off and on, since the 2017 model year, including a 2026 plug-in hybrid, which was a thinly disguised Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV (itself based on the Rogue). This Rogue Hybrid, though, is a new twist for Nissan. It’s not a parallel hybrid like the archrival Toyota RAV4 but a serial hybrid, similar to the sometimes fondly misremembered Chevrolet Volt.

A serial hybrid is, to oversimplify only slightly, an electric powertrain lashed to an internal-combustion engine that acts as a generator to produce current. That current is delivered to a battery and electric motors that do the propulsive work. There is no direct, mechanical drive from engine to road; traction is all delivered electrically. Like a diesel-electric railroad locomotive. That spares buyers the need to live with a constantly variable transmission. For which, hallelujah.

The engine is a 1.5-liter turbocharged three-cylinder making 148 hp and 171 lb-ft in its own right and working in conjunction with a dinky 1.67-kWh lithium-ion battery pack. Drive is delivered through two electric motors, one turning each axle, with a peak system output quoted at 225 hp.

Since this is an electric crossover that happens to have an internal-combustion engine aboard, it drives very much like other electrics. That includes one-pedal driving with regenerative braking in “e-Pedal” mode. It’s more Leaf than Pathfinder or regular Rogue.

Historically, Nissan has done a great job of tuning every Rogue’s suspension for its duty of prowling across every obstacle suburbia throws at it. It crosses Costco speed bumps confidently, doesn’t chunk up when sliding across a curb during parallel parking, and steers precisely and confidently when sneaking into a garage full of bicycles and long disused exercise equipment.

The dry roads of Santa Barbara County in October are no challenge for any all-wheel-drive system. That in mind, the Rogue Hybrid makes effective use of its 235-mm-wide all-season radials (on 18-inch wheels in the base SV and 19s with the SR and Platinum). With much of its battery and electric motor weight carried low, Nissan claims a weight distribution of 56 percent front and 44 percent rear for the test vehicle. The conventional Rogue carries about 60 percent of its weight on its nose.

And then there’s the engine itself. The inline-three runs on the Miller cycle and has a relatively large turbocharger that spools up to keep the engine at its torque peak easily. The engine won’t spin past 5200 rpm, and since all it does is send juice to the motor and battery pack, there was no way for me to push it past that low redline.

This is not a fire-breathing electric. Acceleration is nicely linear as with, say, the Leaf or a Chevrolet Bolt. Because 225 hp can push two tons and then some only so quickly, 0–60 is likely in the mid-six-second range, and the quarter-mile will be just under 16-seconds. It’s roughly comparable to the Leaf.

As nonplussed as the acceleration times will leave those who love to drive, there is the compensation of outstanding fuel economy. The EPA rates the new Rogue Hybrid SR at 41 mpg in the city, 36 mpg on the highway, and 38 mpg combined. That’s up a huge 12 mpg in the city cycle compared with the conventional Rogue Platinum AWD, along with a smaller 4 mpg on the highway and a modest 9 mpg combined.

The rest of the Rogue Hybrid’s mechanical substance is familiar stuff. Many of the structural elements and suspension design carryover from the current conventional Rogue, along with the 106.5-inch wheelbase. The Rogue Hybrid’s 72.8-inch overall width is up 0.4 inch, and the 67.2-inch overall height is down 0.2 inch. Nissan isn’t screwing with what’s working.

Nissan’s interior designers have done an outstanding job of making the new Rogue Hybrid feel roomy. The dash is relatively low below the windshield, and the door panels are shaped for some elbowroom. The seats are also well considered and cushy, which in this class of vehicle is what matters. Eight-way power-adjustable and heated front seats are standard across the line, with the Platinum trim also getting ventilation for cooling and a memory feature. Like giant moonroofs? One comes standard on the Platinum and optional on the lesser trims.

Then there are the Platinum’s massive twin 14.3-inch screens across a common plane. It’s pretty much the same setup as used in the better Leaf models. And the graphics are similar as well. The best feature is the Platinum’s head-up display, which is all kinds of wicked cool.

Also aboard is Nissan’s ProPilot Assist semi-autonomous system, which allows hands-free driving for extended periods. On known, well-marked roads, I found that it worked well.

However, carrying around two powertrains induces pudginess. Nissan lists the conventional 2027 Rogue at between 3444 and 3534 pounds, depending on trim level. The Rogue Hybrid comes in between 4065 and 4167 pounds.

Nissan lists the gross vehicle weight rating of the pure combustion Rogue at 4641 pounds and the Hybrid’s at 5192 pounds. That means that the Hybrid is down in lugging by about 100 pounds—two large suitcases or one large dog. So, pack light and adopt smaller dogs.

The Rogue competes in the toughest part of the current automotive market: compact crossovers. Virtually every manufacturer’s best seller is in this class, with an increasing percentage of the vehicles being hybrid.

Priced across the line to compete with Toyota’s all-hybrid RAV4 line, the Rogue Hybrid is a solid alternative, although the RAV4 AWD is more efficient on every EPA figure. But as Toyota dealers are often constrained by supply issues, so there could be more price flexibility at the Nissan stores.

The other obvious rival is the Honda CR-V Hybrid, which uses a similar but subtly different powertrain from the Rogue Hybrid, this combining a primary electric drive motor with a lockup clutch that can mechanically link the engine to the wheels at higher speeds. The Rogue has a slight advantage on EPA mpg figures when compared with the all-wheel-drive version of the Honda, but the front-wheel-drive CR-V Hybrid is less expensive and better on gas.

The Rogue Hybrid’s nose has an odd funkiness about it. In the SR (with Tech package) that was on hand, most of the upper grille is blocked off. The indentations are more the suggestion of cooling than actual cooling. And the relatively small multipart headlights are surrounded by decorative lighting mostly to balance out the large simulated grille.

#4455. Toyota sells 3 electric SUVs, but which one is best for you?

Toyota now offers three fully electric SUVs: the bZ, C-HR, and bZ Woodland. Here’s how they stack up.

After introducing the new and improved bZ (formerly the bZ4X) in late 2025, the electric SUV quickly became one of the most popular EVs in the US.

In the first nine months of 2026, it was the fourth-best-selling electric vehicle, behind the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

With two additional electric SUVs now on sale, the CH-R and bZ Woodland, Toyota has suddenly become one of America’s top-selling EV brands.

Its EV sales have nearly tripled this year. According to Cox Automotive, Toyota ranked as the third most popular EV brand behind Tesla and Rivian in the third quarter.

Toyota offers three distinct electric vehicles: the 2027 bZ, C-HR, and bZ Woodland, each designed for different lifestyles, so which one is the best fit for you?

After launching the updated model last year, the 2027 bZ starts at $34,980. With the $1,595 delivery fee, the starting price is $36,576.

That’s for the standard 2027 Toyota bZ XLE FWD with an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 236 miles. For longer range, you can upgrade to the FWD Plus model, which offers up to 314 miles and starts at $37,980 (excluding the delivery fee).

The Toyota bZ is available in XLE and Limited grades, with front- or all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrains.

Two battery options are offered: The 57.7 kWh battery on the standard XLE FWD provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 236 miles, while the larger 74.7 kWh battery provides up to 288 miles of range on the XLE AWD and 314 miles on the XLE FWD Plus model.

FWD models produce either 165 hp (XLE FWD) or 221 hp (XLE FWD Plus and Limited FWD), while AWD models deliver a combined 338 hp.

The 2027 bZ also has a built-in NACS port, so you can use Tesla Superchargers without needing a separate adapter. Toyota said it takes around 30 minutes to charge the battery from 10% to 80%.

Inside, the 2027 bZ features Toyota’s updated cabin design. The setup features a 7″ LCD customizable Multi Information Display (MID) and a new 14″ Toyota Audio Multimedia display screen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The bZ is essentially designed as an everyday driver with a long driving range, modern tech, and available AWD.

For those looking for a bigger, more rugged option, the 2027 bZ Woodland may be a better fit. The Woodland is 6″ longer than the standard bZ and comes with standard AWD.

The longer body opens up more interior space, with up to 74.3 cubic feet of storage compared to the bZ with up to 67.1 cubic feet.

Unlike the bZ, the Woodland model has a standard AWD powertrain with Toyota’s X-Mode control system.

The setup delivers a combined 375 horsepower, 37 hp more than the standard bZ, making it Toyota’s most powerful EV currently.

It also adopts a more commanding, upright stance with 8.3″ of ground clearance and 3,500 lbs of towing capacity.

Although it uses the same 74.7 kWh battery as the standard bZ, the Woodland’s EPA-estimated range drops to 281 miles because of the added weight and power. Upgrading to the optional all-terrain tires sacrifices even more range, with up to 260 miles.

Like the bZ, the Woodland also has a built- in NACS port. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes around 30 minutes.

Inside, the bZ Woodland features the same 7″ LCD customizable Multi Information Display (MID) and 14″ Toyota Audio Multimedia display screen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380. All variants include standard roof rails, Dual Qi-capable wireless device chargers, heated front seats and steering wheel, and Digital Key capabilities.

Last, but not least, the C-HR is a smaller, sporty, coupe-like electric SUV. The 2027 Toyota C-HR starts at $37,080, or $2,100 more than the standard bZ.

It’s about 6.7″ shorter than the bZ, with a smaller wheelbase, but also comes with standard AWD. The dual-motor AWD setup delivers a combined 338 hp, not quite as much as the bigger, more powerful Woodland.

The C-HR is available exclusively with the 74.7 kWh battery, which provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 287 miles for the SE grade with 18″ wheels.

Upgrading to 20″ wheels adds a street-ready look but offers slightly less EPA range, with up to 273 miles.

The coupe-like design adds a sleek look and opens up interior space, with up to 59.5 cubic feet of rear cargo space when the rear seats are folded. That’s slightly more than the bZ, which offers up to 56.9 cubic feet.

Inside, the C-HR features the same setup as its other EVs, including a 7″ slim driver’s display and 14″ central infotainment screen.

Like Toyota’s other electric SUVs, the C-HR has a native NACS port. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes about 30 minutes.

These are all basically the same small vehicles. I did not fit in any of them (6’ 2”) it is so frustrating to have less than 300 miles of range on AWD versions that are supposed to be better models.

It is 2026 over a decade since EVs arrived and over 5 years after the Tesla Model Y with practically zero competition almost at same price (Rivian R2 may be next year when affordable versions ship.) BMW, Mercedes and Volvo need $10k more. Hyundai has kept EV5 out of USA.

It is almost like none of the Legacy automakers want any SUV that can compete on price.

The 2027 Toyota C-HR EV is available in two trims: SE and XSE. Standard features include two wireless Qi phone chargers, low-profile roof rails, Fabric/SofTex-trimmed seating, heated front seats and steering wheel, Toyota Safety Sense 3.0, and a power liftgate.

Which Toyota electric SUV would you choose? The bZ, C-HR, or bZ Woodland? Or would you choose another EV? Let us know your pick in the comments. Next year, Toyota will add the Highland EV, its first three-row electric SUV.

#4453. The Mercedes-Benz EQS drove 539 miles on a single charge. Still worried about range?

The new Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ covered 539 miles without stopping to charge, making range anxiety look like a thing of the past.

Mercedes-Benz overhauled the EQS electric sedan, including a bigger battery and an 800V electrical architecture.

The 2027 Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ uses a 122 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 467 miles.

While that’s already impressive, the electric sedan will likely go even farther in everyday driving conditions. During Edmunds recent EV Range Test, the 2027 Mercedes EQS 450+ drove a whopping 539 miles without stopping to charge.

The EQS beat its own EPA estimate by 72 miles and is now the longest-range electric sedan Edmunds has ever tested, beating the Lucid Air, the first EV to break the 500-mile mark. The only EV that has it beat is the Cadillac Escalade IQ, which managed 558 miles from its massive 205 kWh battery.

During the test, the 2027 Mercedes EQS 450+ was also more efficient than its official numbers suggest.

The new EQS used 29.6 kWh per 100 miles, beating its EPA estimate of 28 kWh per 100 miles. In comparison, the 2025 Mercedes EQS 450+ covered 464 miles and used 34 kWh per 100 miles during the same test, so the improvements are considerable.

Edmunds observed a peak charging rate of 350 kW, in line with Mercedes’ estimates, while it sustained an average of 222 kW throughout the session.

Both beat the older EQS, which reached a peak charge rate of 208 kW and sustained an average of 175 kW.

The new Mercedes EQS 450+ added 825 miles of range in an hour, and 100 miles in just over 7 minutes, nearly twice the speed of the 2025MY.

The Edmunds EV Range Test is designed to provide a more accurate estimate of an EV’s range in everyday driving conditions. It includes 60% city and 40% highway driving with an average speed of 40 mph. The vehicle stays within 5 mph of the posted speed limit, and the climate control is set to auto at 72 degrees.

How much is too much? 539 miles on a single charge is impressive, but do you need it? In a recent “nationally representative” survey, BMW found that Americans want more EV range than they actually need.

The study showed that 73% consider 25, 50, or 75 miles enough to cover their daily driving. However, 42% said they would require at least 300 miles of range before they would consider an EV.

If you have access to a home charger, nothing beats waking up with a full charge every day. Meanwhile, public charging continues to improve, giving EV drivers more reliable options on longer trips.

Faster charging also helps. Another 53% said they would be more likely to consider an EV if it could add about 150 miles of range in around 10 minutes.

In the same Edmunds EV Range Test last week, the new 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive drove 436 miles on a single charge, exceeding its EPA estimate of 392 miles by 44 miles. It also used 28.3 kWh per 100 miles during the test, beating its official EPA estimate of 32 kWh per 100 miles.

I'm really glad to see more articles like this and people talking more about efficiency. It's not just about bigger batteries and range. It needs to be about smaller batteries plus great efficiency giving that same range. We need to do this with more efficient designs, more sedans and lighter vehicles.

The new 2027 Volvo EX60 drove 352 miles while the 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric covered 392 miles during the same test.

One thing is certain: electric vehicles are becoming more efficient, enabling longer driving ranges and faster charging times. As battery tech advances, EVs will drive farther and charge faster, while safety and performance will continue to improve.

How much driving range would you consider enough for your daily drive? What about for the week? Let us know in the comments below.

#4452. Ford Tested 36,000 Mustang Mach-E Batteries. Here’s How They Held Up After 100,000 Miles

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

It's one of the top questions I get about EVs: "How long will the battery last?" Understandably, people want to know that their car will go the distance before dropping tens of thousands of dollars on a new car with new-to-them technology.

A growing body of research shows that modern electric cars hold up just fine over years of normal use. And a huge study of Ford Mustang Mach-E SUVs further proves the point.

The Detroit automaker collected battery-health data from 36,000 Mach-E SUVs from the 2021 model year that were sold in the U.S. and Canada. The results, released Monday, should help quiet fears that EVs degrade like smartphones, which struggle to hold a charge after a few years of daily use.

On average, the cars had traveled 55,000 miles over 5.2 years and retained 92% of their usable battery capacity. That means a top-trim 2021 Mustang Mach-E with 305 miles of EPA range would in theory be rated for around 280 miles today. All the cars in the study have nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) battery packs, since Ford didn't introduce a lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery for the Mach-E starting until the 2023 model year.

Ford physically tests cells in the lab and tries to predict battery degradation using computer models before a model launches, Kevin Vander Laan, the automaker's technical leader of high-voltage battery cells and systems, told me in an interview. But the real test comes after a car spends years on the road.

"Our report card slowly trickles in over time," he said. "So here we are with a five-year report card, and it looks great."

Interestingly enough, putting on twice as many miles as average in the same time period barely impacted overall battery health. Ford says the over 2,000 SUVs with more than 100,000 miles on the odometer retained more than 91% of their battery capacity.

Those few drivers who put some 40,000 miles on their Mach-Es each year still had strong battery health after five years. Ford says the 30-plus cars in its dataset that had covered more than 200,000 miles showed 88% battery health.

Of course, these are just averages. So your results may vary depending on lots of factors. EVs that spend their lives in the hot American Southwest tend to age more rapidly than those driven in more temperate climates. Likewise, EV batteries that are frequently fast-charged to 100% and drained to near-empty typically wear out faster than those that are kept in the happy zone of 20% to 80%.

Still, Ford says the distribution of results is encouraging for its battery engineers: It says 95% of the 36,000 cars fell between 87% and 97%.

The results are in line with what other research has uncovered about how EVs age. Some early EVs (notably the first-gen Nissan Leaf) had less sophisticated battery thermal management and saw steep degradation as a result. But modern EVs tend to age far more gracefully.

According to Recurrent, a firm that tracks range retention in used EVs that opt in, the average EV retains 97% of its original observed range after three years and 95% after five years.

In September, battery-health startup Aviloo released the results of 500,000 EV battery tests. After 150,000 kilometers (around 93,000 miles), most models studied showed between 90% and 94% health. The Hyundai Ioniq 5, BMW i4, and Mercedes EQA stood out with readings near the top end of that range. The Mustang Mach-E did just about as well as Ford's own data show: 92.5% battery health. The Tesla Model 3 and Model Y came in at 88.9% and 90.3%, respectively.

Ford makes some familiar recommendations to drivers looking to make sure their EVs last as long as possible. The company says to manage temperature extremes by parking in the shade on scorching days and preconditioning the cabin while the vehicle is plugged in. It also recommends relying on Level 2 charging for daily driving, and using Level 3 DC fast chargers sparingly.

Vander Laan says the learnings from this crop of EVs and how they perform contribute to the development process for Ford's next-generation electric cars, like the sub-$30,000 Fathom pickup coming next year.

"It's really continuous learning," he said. "We have a design that we deeply understand, the data is flowing in, we're learning learning from that, and feeding that to the engineering teams in the company here."

#4451. The Scion Brand Returns to America With a 3-Cylinder Kei Truck for the U.S.

The formerly youth-focused brand is becoming Toyota’s new “freedom lab” for pushing the boundaries of mobility.

Scion lived a short life, the victim of bad financial timing and millennial misunderstandings. But its parent company, Toyota, is about to give the brand another go—and its market research appears to be spot-on this time, as the Japanese automaker announces a new three-cylinder Kei truck for the U.S. market.

Officially known as the Scion Kei-01, the new model takes traditional Japanese compactness and adds North American levels of capability. The heart of the Kei-01 is a 660cc three-cylinder engine paired with a continuously variable transmission and proper four-wheel drive with push-button lock-up. At 11 feet long and five feet wide, the Kei truck will be even smaller than a modern Mini Cooper.

The Kei-01 will be right-hand-drive, have a maximum speed of 25 miles per hour, and is intended to comply with federal safety requirements for low-speed vehicles. An easily accessible three-way fold-down cargo bed, a payload capacity of 600 pounds, and an extended cabin design with a raised roofline were included specifically for the North American market. Scion has not revealed power figures for the Kei-01, but Toyota did confirm the Kei truck will be available in the U.S. market.

Initially, the Kei-01 will arrive in the U.S. as part of a fleet vehicle pilot program. Scion said this new Kei truck will be an intentionally low-volume, niche vehicle for specific kinds of fleets; it’s targeting small business owners looking for an affordable urban commercial vehicle, farmers requiring a dependable daily workhorse, and municipalities, universities, and corporate campuses seeking efficient fleet vehicles. Last-mile delivery services and outdoor enthusiasts are also being targeted by Toyota. Fleet sales will route through select Toyota dealerships, and the truck will be produced at Toyota Motor Manufacturing Indiana in the second half of 2027.

However, Toyota says it is open to expanding availability of the bite-sized pickup. “Based on market conditions, customer demand, and operational considerations, Toyota may consider expanding availability to limited retail sales at a later date. Additional information and the broader sales strategy will be shared as plans are finalized,” the carmaker stated.

Two additional Scion concept vehicles were showcased alongside the Kei-01 at Toyota Motor North America events in Ypsilanti Township, Michigan, and Frisco, Texas, on Tuesday, November 10. The Scion SxS Concept takes on off-roading with a side-by-side frame and a high-output turbocharged four-cylinder hybrid powertrain. The off-road-focused model will feature over 300 horsepower, significant suspension articulation, and a nimble footprint; there will even be a Silent Mode that shifts motive power to the electric drivetrain.

Additionally, Scion is showing off the BKE Concept, a new kind of mobility tool for the revived automotive brand. Packing only two wheels, the BKE Concept is a personal mobility scooter made for the great outdoors. Scion didn’t provide any other details about the BKE Concept, but it appears to be a comfortable urban commuter.

Regardless of the ultimate plans of Scion’s new Kei truck and concept vehicles, the return of the fun-loving brand is worth celebrating. Toyota has been razor-focused on car enthusiasts with its Gazoo Racing and off-road-focused models, and Scion offers another opportunity for enthusiast appeal. But instead of focusing on young buyers exclusively, Scion will be a “freedom lab” for Toyota, with a focus on experimentation.

“The future of mobility will not be defined by one vehicle, one technology or one way of thinking,” said Simon Humphries, chief branding officer, head of design, Toyota Motor Corporation. “Scion by Toyota gives us a place to challenge conventional thinking, explore new possibilities and create mobility in new ways. The KEI-01, SxS, and BKE concepts each represent a different possibility—and together, they show what can happen when curiosity leads the way.”

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4449. PlugShare finally adds dark mode, and there’s more for EV drivers

PlugShare is giving its EV charging app a big overhaul. Version 8.0 arrives worldwide for iPhone on November 10, with dark mode, a trip planner that shows how far apart charging stops are, and a rebuilt Apple Watch app that can point you to a charger compatible with your EV.

Dark mode was one of the most-requested features from PlugShare users. It works across the app and follows your iPhone’s settings, so if your phone switches to dark mode at sunset, your charging map will, too.

The trip planner gets a small but handy change. Each charging stop now shows how far it is from both the start of your trip and the previous stop. So when you’re deciding whether to stretch to the next fast charger or stop sooner, the number you need is right there.

PlugShare now loads your saved locations, trips, and profile when you open the app or sign in, so those tabs are ready to tap. You can also open and zoom in on station photos right from their thumbnails. That’s handy when you’re trying to figure out what corner a charging station is in in a big parking lot. The app also adapts its layout to the iPhone Duo’s different screens and folded positions.

The rebuilt Watch app lists nearby charging stations with distances and directions. It uses the filters you’ve set on your iPhone, so if you’ve filtered for plugs that fit your EV, that carries over to your wrist.

Tap a station and you’ll see its PlugScore, the network that runs it, a small map, and which plugs it has, including NACS, CCS, CHAdeMO, or J1772. The list refreshes when you raise your wrist and open the app. You can also add a shortcut to a round or corner slot on your watch face.

The iPhone update is rolling out through the App Store. PlugShare says Android users will get dark mode and a redesign based on Google’s Material 3 in early 2027.

#4448. This New EV Motor Spins At 30,000 RPM. Here's Why That Matters

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

An electric motor spinning at 30,000 rpm sounds like something you might find in a high-power EV supercar. ZF has something less extravagant in mind: making the hardware that powers everyday EVs smaller, lighter, and less hungry for expensive materials.

ZF’s new High Revolution Drive combines the motor, power electronics, and transmission all in the same housing. Unlike Mercedes-Benz, though, it doesn't also put the brakes inside the same housing.

Compared with one of ZF’s comparable Select drive units, which spins up to 18,000 rpm, the company claims nearly 25% less weight and volume, half the magnet mass, and a similar efficiency of almost 93%.

This helps because less mass improves EV range, and fewer magnets reduce costs and supply-chain dependence.

According to ZF, spinning the motor faster lets it deliver the same power from a smaller, lighter package. Gears then reduce that speed and increase the turning force sent to the wheels, using a reduction ratio of about 18:1. The version ZF showed produces up to 268 horsepower, with the gearing delivering peak torque of 2,581 pound-feet (3,500 Nm) to the wheels.

The torque measurement comes after the gearing has multiplied the motor’s output. The “two-stage transmission” doesn’t actually mean a two-speed gearbox. It describes successive gear reductions, not two separate driving ratios.

The company says the production High Revolution Drive should deliver 200 to 268 hp and work with both 400- and 800-volt platforms. Reusing its modular Select architecture should simplify installation, shorten development and control costs, and retain manufacturing flexibility. Talks with automakers are underway, with production targeted by 2030.

ZF isn’t alone in trying to squeeze more useful output from a smaller package. One prototype of Yasa’s ultra-compact axial-flux motor produced over 1,000 hp and weighed just 28 pounds. That’s its short-term peak figure, with continuous output estimated at 469–536 bhp.

Yasa’s figure describes only the motor, while ZF’s weight reduction refers to the whole integrated drive unit. Gearing and power electronics still need somewhere to live, and they also add weight.

ZF has also introduced repair kits intended to let workshops fix individual drive unit components, such as gearbox bearings, instead of replacing entire assemblies. That addresses a different problem from shrinking and making hardware lighter, but one buyers may care about considerably more once the warranty expires.

However, ZF hasn’t said whether these two developments are connected, or whether the kits it revealed should be taken as a repairability promise for this new drive. There’s also no mention of which production EV would get this new drive unit. We also don’t know whether those engineering gains will remain unchanged from today’s announcement to something you can actually buy.

Still, this kind of EV development deserves attention even without a four-figure horsepower claim. A family car doesn’t need to break acceleration records, but making its drive unit lighter and less expensive (and possibly easier to repair, too) is exactly what it needs. Whether any savings reach buyers is another question, but giving cars the same power with smaller and less hardware is a good place to start.

#4447. Drive with Style: Our Favorite Chronographs & Driving Watches (Mostly) under $1000

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Whether you’re buying a gift for a car lover or just looking to step up your style, check out our favorite watches and chronographs for drivers.

This story was updated in November 2026 with new products and fresh information.

As a watch enthusiast, I know all too well the dilemma friends, partners, and family members face when trying to buy a watch as a gift. Watch people can be incredibly particular. We obsess over case sizes, movements, bracelet designs, dial layouts, and brand history in the same way car enthusiasts argue over engine codes or wheel specs.

That’s what makes this list different. These aren’t cheap knockoffs or forgettable department-store watches. Instead, they’re enthusiast-focused timepieces that capture the spirit, heritage, and personality that make great watches special, without requiring luxury-watch money.

I’ve rounded up a nice selection of vintage-inspired chronographs, quirky design icons, and motorsport-influenced watches that genuine enthusiasts will appreciate, wear often, and happily give real wrist time to long after the wrapping paper is gone.

The Timex Atelier Chronograph Quartz M1q brings a more considered design approach to an accessible everyday chronograph. Its balanced 40mm stainless-steel case, refined subdial layout, and engraved black dial give it a premium look without feeling overly busy, while a double-curved sapphire crystal adds a welcome touch of durability. A Swiss-made quartz chronograph movement keeps time accurately, without the added cost or maintenance of an automatic, and the tachymeter scale offers a useful nod to traditional motorsport watches. It’s available with either an oil- and chemical-resistant NBR rubber strap or a self-adjusting stainless-steel bracelet, and its 100-meter water resistance makes it practical beyond the watch box.

The PRS 516 features a 42mm case, perforated leather strap, and piston-inspired pushers, all nodding directly to Sixties motorsport, while the Swiss automatic chronograph movement underneath gives it legitimate credibility. Tissot has been tied to racing for decades, and the PRS 516 leans into that heritage without feeling like a costume piece. It’s sporty, tactile, and busy in the best possible way.

The Timex Marlin Neo Classic Chronograph takes one of the brand’s most recognizable vintage designs and gives it a cleaner, more streamlined look. Its compact 40mm brushed stainless-steel case, polished top ring, and curved pushers preserve the Marlin’s mid-century character, while three dial and strap combinations offer slightly different takes on the same retro-inspired design. Details like the domed acrylic crystal, multiscale dial markings, and tachymeter scale give it the feel of a vintage instrument watch without making it overly busy. Inside, a quartz chronograph movement provides accurate, low-maintenance timekeeping and a functional stopwatch, making the Neo Classic a handsome everyday option for anyone drawn to classic watch design.

The Form C feels like the automotive equivalent of a stripped-down Bauhaus sports coupe: clean, lightweight, and engineered with restraint. Its 40mm stainless-steel case wears slim, thanks to Junghans’s minimalist German design language, while the calfskin leather strap keeps things understated and comfortable. A reliable quartz chronograph movement fits the watch’s no-nonsense personality and gives it dead-simple usability. Junghans’s heritage stretches back to 1861, and the Form C channels that legacy into a watch that’s more about precision and proportion than flash.

The Seiko Prospex Speedtimer SSC947 pairs motorsport heritage with modern tech in a 41.4 mm stainless-steel case with brushed and polished finishing. Powered by Seiko’s solar V192 movement, it offers a chronograph, 24-hour subdial, power-reserve indicator, and date display, with a six-month reserve when fully charged. The 947 model is my favorite version of the Speedtimer, with its awesome yellow dial. Protected by a curved sapphire crystal with inner antireflective coating and mounted on a three-link stainless bracelet, it’s water-resistant to 100 meters. Seiko’s reputation as a favorite among horologists speaks to the brand’s consistent quality, innovation, and mechanical mastery, making the SSC947 a reliable and stylish choice for both collectors and racing enthusiasts alike.

If the yellow dial is a bit too bold, you can also check out the SSC943 in Ivory and Green, and the panda-dialed SSC813.

Nicknamed the “Bullhead,” the Tsuno Chronograph wears its motorsport inspiration proudly, with its pushers mounted at the top of the 45mm case like vintage rally timers. Citizen revived the design from the brand’s iconic Seventies Bullhead chronographs, combining retro styling with modern Eco-Drive solar-powered quartz tech that eliminates battery changes. It’s bold, unapologetically funky, and one of the most distinctive modern chronographs you can buy without crossing into luxury-watch pricing.

Featuring a 41mm stainless-steel case with brushed and polished surfaces, this Alpina Startimer is powered by a quartz chronograph movement. A large “Big Date” window sits at 6 o’clock, and a 100-meter water-resistance rating ensures a bit of water won’t be a worry. The white dial sports bold numerals, luminous hands, and a red-triangle chronograph seconds hand, and it is protected by a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal. It comes with a three-link stainless-steel bracelet and delivers chronograph utility in a clean, sporty package.

The Conquest Chronograph features a 42mm stainless-steel case, ceramic tachymeter bezel, and automatic chronograph movement, striking an excellent balance between luxury and sportiness. Longines has deep roots in timing motorsport and aviation events dating back over a century, and the Conquest channels that pedigree into a polished, well-rounded package.

The Bulova Racer 150th Anniversary Shelby pairs motorsport style with serious precision. Powered by Precisionist movement, it delivers exceptional accuracy and a smooth sweeping second hand, plus a 1/1000-second chronograph for track-ready performance. The bold blue dial, sapphire crystal, and 43mm stainless-steel case channel classic racing design, while the lightweight striped rubber strap keeps it comfortable for everyday wear. Rugged, refined, and collector-worthy, this limited-edition timepiece is engineered to stand out.

The Bulova Racer Chronograph stands out thanks to its sharp case lines, bold subdials, and an aggressive motorsport-inspired aesthetic. Its stainless-steel case measures around 42mm and pairs with a sporty bracelet setup, while the quartz chronograph movement emphasizes precision and practicality. Bulova’s long history in American watchmaking, including timing innovations and racing partnerships, gives the Racer more authenticity than its flashy styling initially suggests.

The Legacy Tonneau Chronograph has a distinctly Seventies flavor, with its curved rectangular case shape and integrated-bracelet-inspired design evoking vintage sports watches of the era. Timex keeps things simple with a quartz chronograph movement and stainless-steel construction that prioritizes durability and affordability over pretense. The tonneau-shaped case wears differently from traditional round chronographs, giving it a cool retro personality. It’s proof that enthusiast-oriented design doesn’t have to come with a luxury-watch price tag

The Citizen Eco-Drive Weekender Brycen Chronograph is a sharp, 44 mm watch with a bold blue dial that looks great on the wrist. It’s powered by light, so you never need to change a battery, and it packs a chronograph, 12/24‑hour time, a date window, and 100-meter water resistance. Stylish, tough, and low-maintenance, it’s perfect for everyday wear or weekend adventures.

The Ventura Chrono is pure mid-century Americana. Its asymmetrical 32.3mm-by-50.3mm triangular case design became iconic after Elvis Presley famously wore one, and Hamilton has kept the look alive with modern chronograph hardware and a supple leather strap. Powered by a quartz chronograph movement, the Ventura trades traditional racing-watch cues for style and wrist presence. It’s like a Sixties concept car brought to life.

The Swatch New Chrono takes a lighthearted approach to a chronograph, with a 43mm stainless‑steel case, intuitive chronograph subdials, a tachymeter bezel, and a reliable Swiss quartz movement. Whether you’re timing sprint starts or simply want a watch that looks dynamic on your wrist, this piece combines accessible build quality, youthful design cues, and a distinctive racing-inspired spirit.

This iconic watch retains the classic Marlin Sixties design features that make it so cool and timeless. With a domed acrylic crystal lens and retro-style square markers at 3, 9, and 12 o'clock, it features a natural leather strap and a tachymeter index along its outer minute track to measure speed. We dig the racing stripes on this blue version, but many face and band combinations are available.

Built for serious outdoor missions, this timepiece features a rugged 45mm Carbonox case, unidirectional bezel, and 300-meter water resistance, ready for land, sea, or whatever the trail throws at you. With 18 tritium light tubes that ensure visibility for up to 25 years, an orange screw-in crown, and the “Never Give Up” motto engraved on the caseback alongside Bear Grylls’s signature, it combines Swiss precision with no-compromise practicality.

Featuring a distinctive square resin case, the AE1200WHD‑1A is a retro‑futuristic digital watch built for function and value. It offers world time across 31 time zones (48 cities + UTC), a 1/100‑second stopwatch, a countdown timer, five daily alarms, and a full auto‑calendar up to 2099. With an impressively long 10‑year battery life, 100-meter water resistance, LED backlight, and a stainless‑steel bracelet, it is the perfect beater watch for a seasoned horologist or a gateway drug to the uninitiated.

The Timex Q Chronograph blends vintage charm with modern functionality in a stainless-steel 38mm case that channels late-Seventies sports-watch aesthetics. Powered by a quartz chronograph movement, it features a day-date window, a rotating bezel, and subtle retro accents such as a distressed leather strap.

#4446. Humble Hauler autonomous trailer takes the truck out of trucking [update]

Less than a year after its founding, truckless trucking brand Humble Robotics has secured more than $75 million after a $51 million Series A funding round that will fuel the company’s transition from prototype to preproduction.

The latest funding round for the driverless, cab-less, and truck-less battery-electric freight platform developer was led by Obvious Ventures with participation from other existing investors Eclipse and Energy Impact Partners. Humble said it will use the funding for customer pilots, testing and validation, and early manufacturing.

“We’ve spent years proving that a truck can drive itself,” explains Humble Robotics founder and CEO, Eyal Cohen. “The harder question is how to make autonomy something a freight operator can depend on every day.”

We originally covered the Humble Hauler back in May. You can check out the original article, below, then let us know what you think of the company’s prospects in the comments.

The startup that dares to ask, “Why does the Macbook driving my freight around need a whole cab?” just showed off a fully driverless, cab-less, and truck-less battery-electric freight platform designed to handle containerized cargo more efficiently than ever.

Instead of looking at the tractor and asking how to make it work without a driver, Humble looked at the trailer, itself, redesigning the container chassis as a vehicle from the ground up. The end result isn’t just an autonomous solution, it’s an overall lighter platform without a cab that saves shippers the weight of a sleeper cab, a day cab, or the truck at all.

The Humble approach is said to improve payload efficiency of shipping containers, and intended for dock-to-dock operation.

“I have dedicated my career to building electric and autonomous vehicle technology,” explains Eyal Cohen, Humble Robotics’ founder and CEO. “For the first time, freight can be fully automated all the way to the loading dock. We are making freight sustainable, safe and efficient in a way no one thought was possible. And we’re doing it with an exceptional team of industry veterans and AV experts.”

Emerging from stealth after a $24 million funding round, Humble claims to have completed its first Humble Hauler prototype in less than six months – and they’ll soon be ready to begin autonomous testing in pilot programs with a number of logistics partners.

The vehicle uses a combination of cameras, lidar, and radar for 360-degree awareness (unhindered by seeing around a cab), and uses vision-language-action models to help the system respond to new scenarios.

Thanks to superior battery tech, a maturing global charging infrastructure, and a permanently damaged MidEast oil supply, there’s never been a better time to be an EV startup. Humble is hitting all the electric trailer buzzwords, too, while also touting the fact that the electric powertrain can reduce a company’s to volatile fuel prices even as it helps produce other cost benefits like lower maintenance costs.

There is a reason why the transportation industry developed separate cabs and trailers. Trailers can be loaded or unloaded for days and are much less expensive than trucks that serve both purposes in one piece. That allows the more expensive piece of the transport puzzle to be used more and allows the trailer to be loaded and unloaded while the cab is elsewhere working or in the shop. Query whether the savings they cite will surpass the costs of not having the flexibility of a cab and trailer design.

And if a robot like this can deliver on its promises without the baked-in inefficiencies of humanoids, they might be one step closer to provide that the most efficient solution to a problem is rarely a general one, and even rarer is it a solution that looks like a human.

#4445. 2027 Chevrolet Silverado HD, a Gorilla-Strong Pickup You Don’t Have to Wrestle With

A monstrously torquey new 8.3-liter turbo-diesel V-8 and new electric power steering make this heavy-duty pickup easy to drive.

The lightest Atlas stone used in international strongman competitions is 220 pounds. The heaviest is nearly 500 pounds. Extremely large, frighteningly strong people lift these big orbs onto shoulder-high plinths, and just watching it will give you an inferiority complex—and sciatica. Luckily, there’s a way to feel a similar sense of broad-shouldered accomplishment without spending a lifetime in the gym. Drive the 2027 Chevy Silverado Heavy-Duty (HD) pickup, preferably with a trailer attached, and you’ll get the same rush of endorphins as 2026 World Strongest Man champion Mitchell Hooper as he lifted spheres and repped deadlifts of over 800 pounds.

While the 2027 Silverado 1500 got a full redesign for 2027, the HD is mostly carryover in body and interior. Still, it has some new delights, the biggest and most delightful being the new 8.3-liter Duramax V-8 turbo-diesel engine. This big brute belts out 555 horsepower and 1230 pound-feet of torque, is backed by a 10-speed automatic transmission, and makes light work of towing even the heaviest trailer.

See all results for new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 2500HD / 3500HD for sale near 20147

To keep the burly engine happy, the HD trucks have a revised cooling system with a four-deep stack of radiators, charge coolers, and oil coolers. To keep the driver cool when stopping a fully loaded HD pickup, 14.6-inch front brake rotors clamped by four-piston calipers replace the outgoing model’s two-piston binders. An electronic brake booster, a first for a heavy-duty pickup, gives the brake pedal a similar feel to what you’d find in a regular SUV, no heavy foot needed for effective braking.

To demonstrate the diesel’s grunt, Chevy hooked up a massive trailer loaded with construction equipment and let us rip, towing nearly 37,000 pounds down a drag strip. The new trucks are rated for up to 38,000 pounds with a gooseneck trailer (when equipped with the Max Trailering package). The NHRA won’t be adding a sled-pulling class to its competition anytime soon, but the big truck moved out with barely a shudder, and the upgraded brakes and e-booster made stopping at the far end as easy as launching. The most intimidating part of the pull was making the turnout at the end of the strip, but the HD’s smooth power delivery and redesigned steering made for a drama-free turn despite the tight corner.

The 2500 HD lineup encompasses six trims, starting with the WT (Work Truck) and topping out with the optioned-up High Country. The base engine remains a 6.6-liter gas-burning V-8 (distinct from the similarly sized optional V-8 in redesigned 2027 light-duty models), albeit updated to now develop 412 horsepower and 472 pound-feet of torque. The new Duramax V-8 is an $11,400 option, and it’s available on all trims. That’s a big jump from the outgoing 6.6-liter diesel V-8, which added only $9990 to the HD’s price. Luckily for truck shoppers, overall starting prices see a smaller price hike. The MSRP for the 2027 WT begins at $49,995 (an increase of $1000 versus 2026), and the High Country now starts at $78,195.

See all results for new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 2500HD / 3500HD for sale near 20147

Step up into the cabin—or haul yourself up with the grab handle—and you’ll find the interior is little changed from 2026 models. It’s spacious and cushy with big storage compartments, but the design and the dash layout are the same as before. What is new is some of the software available through the 13.4-inch center touchscreen. There’s an updated Tow/Haul mode that fine-tunes power delivery, shift points, and braking to make for smoother towing up and downhill. An Off-Road mode allows more wheelspin to prevent bog-downs, and off-road-oriented ZR2 HDs get the same Terrain mode as the light-duty version, a trail-focused tune that teams the throttle with automatic braking for what’s essentially one-pedal driving during off-roading. Optional camera add-ons make for up to 14 different views, including an invisible-trailer mode and a split screen when reversing. In the various camera views, the HD lacks the light duty’s helpful graphic overlays, but it’s probably fair to assume that buyers of heavy-duty trucks aren’t beginners at towing.

Another feature that has not made its way from light duty to heavy duty is Chevy’s Super Cruise hands-free driving. In the past, this was because the HD still used a hydraulic steering system, but a major change for 2027 is the switch to electric power steering. The new rack-and-pinion electric steering setup is another first for the HD, and it makes a big difference in the feedback through the wheel and consistency of steering feel even during braking and hard steering inputs. It gives the HD a more consumer-friendly feel. On a mountain road, these big rigs feel manageable, and while you still won’t want to swing a tight U-turn, there’s no fighting the wheel when changing direction. While this year’s trucks won’t offer Super Cruise, the technology is in place for GM to fit additional driver aids in the future.

That omission aside, the theme of the HDs’ changes for 2027 is ease of use. Most of what’s new isn’t visible from the outside, but it’s all designed to make the tasks of hauling and towing feel less like a job and more like a cruise in a passenger vehicle—a really burly passenger vehicle.

#4444. Ford's Radical New EV Manufacturing Process Is Already Building Trucks

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

During its recent quarterly earnings call, one Ford executive revealed that it has already begun rolling Fathoms off the line at its recently revamped factory in Louisville well ahead of the affordable electric pickup's late-2027 delivery schedule.

"It's progressing very well," said Ford COO, Kumar Galhotra, during the company's recent quarterly earnings call. "90% of the validation testing has been completed. We've built our first production line vehicles at Louisville assembly plant."

Importantly, Galhotra didn't say these are production vehicles. Rather, these are the first Fathoms built on their real production line. Essentially, these validation vehicles are the beginning of Ford proving out its production process for both the Fathom and its Universal Electric Vehicle Platform. It's an important milestone for Ford, which has bet its electric future on the UEV platform and a radically different method of manufacturing cars than it's used before.

Ford will build the Fathom using a so-called "assembly tree" rather than the assembly line Henry Ford pioneered a century ago. The front, middle, and rear sections of the pickup will be put together simultaneously, then joined together toward the end of the process. Ford says this should allow it to build vehicles quicker and more efficiently, in part by making the ergonomics better for its workers. It resembles the "unboxed" process Tesla has introduced for the Cybercab.

Ford has been building cars for more than a century, but a new EV on a new platform using new manufacturing techniques needs to be fleshed out—especially if Ford wants to quickly hit the production volumes it's reportedly targeting: 100,000 sales in the first year. As Tesla CEO Elon Musk said in the midst of the company's period of production hell: "It's relatively easy to make a prototype, but extremely difficult to mass manufacture a vehicle reliably at scale."

The testing isn't just limited to the Louisville plant where more than $2 billion was invested to manufacture the Fathom. Ford's Shelbyville Technical Center has also been cranking out large castings used to underpin its affordable electric pickup.

These large castings are made in a similar way to Tesla's Gigacasting process with the goal being to cut down on the production complexity (and cost) of the Fathom. In total, it takes 146 different parts into just 2 large castings. Galhotra says that Ford has already made 5,000 of these unicastings and has effectively substantiated its ability to build this new tech at a high rate.

The next challenge, according to the COO, is the rest of the supply chain:

"We need to make sure that the supply base can run at rate with high quality parts," said Galhotra "And that's very normal at this stage of the launch, and that's what we're going to be working on for the next few months."

The Blue Oval doesn't plan on delivering any of these pickups for about a year, which means that it still has time to ramp things up and make sure the so-called "assembly tree" is running smoothly. The Fathom could prove out to be Ford's EV redemption arc if the automaker gets it right. Affordable? Check. Versatile? Check. Scalable? That's to be seen.

#4443. How the cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas

An international team of researchers, led by Jonathan Freundlich (University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory), has revealed how a dense cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas. By mapping the molecular gas in a galaxy group located 7 billion light-years away, they found that the galaxies in this group harbor, on average, gas reservoirs reduced by more than half compared to similar isolated galaxies. The results of this study are published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

#4442. Honda shows off its next electric motorcycle, and it’s wilder than you thought

Honda has been getting increasingly serious about electric motorcycles, but if you want to see just how weird the company thinks the future could get, take a look at the Honda EV Outlier Concept.

I got a chance to see the wild-looking machine in person at EICMA in Milan, where it looked like almost nothing else on the show floor. And that’s exactly the point.

The EV Outlier Concept originally debuted at last year’s Japan Mobility Show as Honda’s attempt to imagine an electric motorcycle that isn’t simply a conventional motorcycle with the engine swapped for a battery and motor. In fact, Honda describes the concept as looking toward the future of electric motorcycles beyond 2030.

Instead of a centrally mounted motor driving the rear wheel, the EV Outlier uses motors inside both wheels, giving it all-wheel drive and allowing Honda’s designers to completely rethink the rest of the motorcycle’s layout. The battery is housed in that large central black body, while the rider sits extremely low and behind it.

Honda describes the design philosophy with three words: “Gliding, Ecstasy, and Low.” The first refers to the smooth, nearly silent feeling of electric propulsion, while the second describes the instant acceleration and massive torque available from independently controlled front and rear motors. “Low” is more literal: Honda deliberately dropped the rider’s seating and eye position to create an entirely different sensation from a conventional motorcycle.

There’s even a bucket-style backrest designed to support the rider under hard acceleration and let the rider pivot through corners around their hips.

Cool and fun for Honda engineers to play with, but it seems a big no for reality, or at least a different road reality then mine.

Emergency tight swerves for accident avoidance? Nope, gone. Seeing even less of the road, even without a car in front of you, due to being so low? Not good for me nor the deer I don't avoid due to seeing it too late.

Unsprung mass due to hub motors - lots of literature on that topic, so I'll leave that alone.

Up front, traditional mirrors are replaced by cameras, while a wide digital cockpit can display things like lean angle, riding modes, front motor torque adjustment, and what the two wheels are doing in real time.

Will Honda actually build this thing? Almost certainly not exactly as you see it here. That’s what concepts are for.

But the EV Outlier is still interesting as a statement of intent. Honda is obviously still playing around with the freedom that electric drivetrains offer, and the company is asking what motorcycles could become once designers no longer have to work around engines, fuel tanks, transmissions, and traditional drivetrains.

And judging by what I saw at EICMA, Honda’s answer could get pretty wild.

#4441. Toyota Tundra Driver Hits 130 MPH in Police Chase, Then Claims He Was Asleep in the Back Seat: Cops

Police say the driver jumped in the back while the truck was spinning after a PIT maneuver, then tried to convince them he had nothing to do with the chase.

Police officers have heard all sorts of excuses from speeders, from trying to get to work on time to running late for a haircut. Chances are, whatever excuse you try, the police have heard it before. That said, a Toyota Tundra driver that police say recently lead them on a 130-mile-per-hour chase in Florida may have tried the most unique excuse ever: according to Gulf Coast News, the man claimed he was sleeping in the back seat the whole time.

WINK News reports that a Collier County Sheriff's Office Corporal saw a beige Toyota Tundra at about 2:20 a.m. running over a curb while attempting to get to a gas station in Naples, Florida. The Toyota reportedly refused to stop for police; a chase ensued, and authorities claim the truck hit speeds of 130 mph in 45-mile-per-hour zones—impressive velocity, for a Tundra. Deputies reportedly deployed stop sticks, successfully puncturing the Tundra's tires, but that still didn’t end the chase; authorities say it took a PIT maneuver to finally bring the truck to a halt.

Then, it seems, things took an odd turn. According to the arrest report, a passenger told deputies that the driver, identified as Oswaldo Perez-Ramirez, jumped from the driver's seat into the back seat—while the truck was spinning after the PIT maneuver. When officers questioned Perez-Ramirez, he reportedly insisted he hadn't been driving at all; in fact, he allegedly claimed he'd been sleeping in the back seat.

However, that story fell apart when police reviewed the dashcam video, and it showed the driver wearing a white shirt; Perez-Ramirez was also wearing a white shirt when officers removed him from the truck, police say. He was subsequently arrested and faces charges of fleeing and eluding, fleeing and eluding at a high rate of speed, driving without a valid license, failure to stop, and DUI.
