#4329. 10 Pokémon Characters Who Deserved Much More Attention

Laurence Wall is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been writing professionally since 2022 and covering games since 2023. He primarily writes guides and lists, with a focus on indie games, RPGs, ARPGs, Soulslikes, MMOs, card games, boss fights, and detailed tutorials. Before joining DualShockers, Laurence worked as

While Pokémon is best known for the Pokémon themselves, every game brings an eclectic cast of characters we interact with as Pokémon trainers. Whether it’s quirky Gym Leaders, angsty rivals, or just odd folks you meet along the way, your journey is punctuated by these interesting experiences.

This list covers some of the best things players find when taking their time in the Pokémon series.

However, sometimes a character comes along that really makes you pay attention. Maybe it’s the way they look, what they said, or the Pokémon they used, but they stick in your memory somehow. The Pokémon series is full of these characters. More often than not, they appear and disappear as fast as they were introduced, leaving you a little confused about why they didn’t play a bigger role.

Here are a few examples of characters I wish had a bigger role, or were fleshed out a bit more over the course of all nine Generations to date.

Anyone who played the original Diamond and Pearl back in the day will remember Cheryl. She’s the helpful trainer who accompanies you through Eterna Forest, right before the second gym. You might think she doesn’t have much of a role, since all she does is heal your Pokémon with her Chansey and then wander off, yet she seems to recur throughout the franchise.

Cheryl reappears later in the Battleground, a place generally reserved for powerful trainers, with a team of Pokémon with crazy-high HP stats, and also in the Battle Tower. She also appears in Pokémon Generations, getting lost in The Old Chateau, and seems to have a relative in Hisui called Sabi.

It’s a shame we never got to see a bit more from Cheryl in the story, or even in something like Pokémon Contests!

Mohn has always been a pretty interesting character in Pokémon Sun and Moon. You’ll originally meet him when you’re introduced to the Poke Pelago; however, you might notice he looks a little familiar.

Long story short, Mohn was originally a researcher at the Aether Foundation and Lusamine's husband. However, when we meet him, he’s unfortunately lost his memory. It’s rumoured that when researching the Ultra Wormholes, he fell into one and developed amnesia, but this topic isn’t really explored much.

I would have loved a bit more backstory about Mohn, his relationship with his family and just what happened to him when travelling through Ultra Space. However, we may never know.

Marley, like Cheryl, is a Generation 4 character we meet while exploring a certain area of the game. This area is an offshoot of Victory Road and can only be explored in the Post-Game.

Marley doesn’t like to talk much and seems very caring. As such, while she does have an Arcanine, it’s also equipped with Helping Hand to assist you in battle. Like Cheryl, she can also be found in the Battleground and the Battle Tower, and she specialises in high-speed Pokémon.

The thing is, Marley obviously has a connection to Shaymin, which the game doesn’t really develop much. She helps us reach Seabreak Path and can even be found there again if you bring Oak’s Letter. On top of this, in Pokémon Masters, she even has a Shaymin! Is she just an interested trainer, or is there more to it?

Malva is the Fire-type Elite Four member of the Kalos region. Most Elite Four members don’t have much to offer, aside from an interesting design. However, Malva is hiding something far more sinister beneath the surface.

From Ultra Necrozma’s stat boosts to Volo’s grueling final battle, these Pokémon encounters bend the rules to deliver memorable challenges.

See, Malva is actually part of the heinous Team Flare, which you work to dismantle throughout the game. We learn later, in Legends Z-A, that Malva was there when they captured the legendary Pokémon Yveltal and helped take it down.

This is why she seems so prickly towards you when you face her in the Pokémon League. I would have liked to see a bit more of Malva and learn more about her involvement with Team Flare. The Flare storyline always seemed a bit weak after all.

Thankfully, Malva seems to learn her lesson and helps us with Dr Xerosic in the X and Y postgame, somewhat redeeming herself.

Benga is a really odd character. He’s obviously the Grandson of the Champion, Alder; that’s pretty obvious from his radical hairstyle. However, it’s never explained how Benga got so powerful. More so than his Grandfather, the Champion, might I repeat!

Benga is the final boss of the White Treehollow in White 2 or the Black Tower in Black 2. As such, he has an absolutely ludicrous team of Latios/Latias, Garchomp/Dragonite, and a Volcarona. While the Volcarona is obviously a nod to Alder, how on earth did this little kid get his hands on a pair of legendaries?

Once you’ve defeated him, you can head back to Floccesy Town, where Benga will offer you either a Shiny Gible or a Shiny Dratini. Now he seems to have shiny Pokémon to offer you, but how did he get these? This kid is a real mystery.

Starting in Generation 5, you can find Ingo in the Battle Subway, where he serves as a main boss alongside his brother Emmet. And for a long time, that’s where he stayed. A fairly obscure, relatively uninteresting character who didn’t draw much attention.

However, you might be surprised to come across Ingo in Hisui, in Pokémon Legends: Arceus. And no, this isn’t some ancient relative like most other Sinnoh trainers; this really is Ingo, having travelled through time and lost a good chunk of his memories. But why him, and not a Sinnoh character?

Thankfully, Ingo gets a happy ending, as we learn in Legends Z-A that he eventually returned to Unova and reunited with his brother Emmet. Turns out even the most unassuming trainer can have their secrets!

And speaking of people being zapped across Space and Time, here we have Anabel. We were originally introduced to Anabel in Pokémon Emerald, where she served as a Frontier Brain, one of the most powerful and difficult trainers in the entire series.

After defeating the Elite Four, these are the Pokémon Games Where the Post-Game Feels Like a Whole New Adventure.

However, fast-forward to Pokémon Sun and Moon, and we meet Anabel again; like Ingo, she’s been mysteriously transported to Alola, this time through an Ultra Wormhole rather than by Arceus. Now she’s part of the International Police, and as part of the UB task force, she’s there to round up the rabid Ultra Beasts rampaging across the region.

We know Anabel is a strong trainer, before and after the incident, but how did she enter the Ultra Wormhole in the first place? Was she chosen? Or was it just random chance? We never really get an answer here. It would have been nice to get a little more backstory into what happened in Hoenn.

Zinnia appears only in the Generation 3 remakes, Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire. During the adventure, you run into her masquerading as part of the evil team, but you soon learn she’s actually part of an ancient group trying to summon Rayquaza.

She plays a larger role in the Delta Episode; however, all her efforts are for nothing, as the main character ends up Mega Evolving Rayquaza and stopping the Meteor.

Zinnia has a fantastic, interesting design, and the bits and pieces we get of her backstory make it seem like she’ll play a bigger role in the story. She seems to know so much more than we do, especially about the Pokémon Multiverse, but again, we never fully explore her story. At least we still have that incredible battle theme!

If you’ve played Pokémon Colosseum or XD, you’ll have fond memories of this utterly bizarre trainer. Miror B is a funky villain and one of the four admins of Team Cipher. However, you’ll quickly notice that while he might be on the bad side, his real passion is actually dancing!

And not only does he like to bust a move, but his Pokémon do too! And, I have to admit, he’s got one of the best battle songs in the entire Pokémon series! The cool thing about Miror B is that, once defeated, he actually leaves Team Cipher in order to set up his own group, whom you meet in the sequel. He might never quite renounce his wicked ways, but for entertainment, you don’t get much better than this.

It’s certainly a shame we never got to see more of Miror B, as Game Freak seems determined to ignore Genius Sonority’s twin masterpieces.

Yep, this is one for the OGs. I remember back in Primary school, when rumours of Mew being under the truck were still floating around, there was another rumour about the dark side of the kind and generous Mr. Fuji.

The thing is, this one actually holds water, unlike the Mew story. You first find Mr. Fuji in Lavender Town, looking after orphaned Pokémon, and defending the Marowak from Team Rocket in Pokémon Tower. We later learn that Mr. Fuji and Blaine were good friends, and that they both worked on a project in the burned-down Pokémon Mansion over on Cinnabar.

Of course, the theory is that Mr. Fuji was one of the scientists who created Mewtwo through genetic experimentation on Mew. He was so traumatised by his creation that he vowed never to hurt a Pokémon again, and moved to Lavender Town to atone for his misdeeds.

This theory is reflected in the Pokémon Origins series and in Dr. Fuji in Mewtwo Strikes Back. We also know Mr. Fuji travelled to Faraway Island and left a note for the trainer before they find Mew. Was this the original Mew used to create Mewtwo?

However, I'm fairly certain we never actually got the official answer to this theory in the mainline games. For now, we’ll have to rely on theories to sate our appetite for Pokémon lore! Maybe one day we’ll know for sure?

From NPC placements to move typings, these are the Pokémon FireRed & LeafGreen Changes That Quietly Improved the Original Games.

#4328. Caltech robot makes history by building a structure in space

For the first time, a robot has successfully assembled part of a structure in space without astronauts, demonstrating a technology that could dramatically change how large spacecraft and scientific instruments are built.

The robotic system was developed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) with funding from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). It is part of DARPA's Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program, an initiative exploring ways to manufacture and assemble enormous structures directly in space.

Rather than relying on astronauts to connect individual pieces, the robot uses an automated arm to retrieve structural tubes and connecting joints from nearby storage dispensers. It then joins the components into repeating sections, called bays, that form a larger supporting framework known as a truss.

"This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space," says Sergio Pellegrino, the Joyce and Krent Kresa Professor of Aerospace and Civil Engineering, the Lynn Booth and Kent Kresa Department of Aerospace Leadership Chair, the executive officer for aerospace, and a senior research scientist at JPL, which Caltech manages for NASA.

A Historic Step Toward Building Giant Structures in Space

Pellegrino leads Caltech's Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA) demonstration. The robotic system has spent six months in orbit attempting to construct a reflector antenna measuring 1.4 meters across. Its design combines composite fiber tubes, aluminum connectors, and a lightweight reflective surface made from Kapton, a durable polymer film commonly used in spacecraft.

DARPA compares the assembly process to building with sophisticated versions of K'Nex or Tinkertoy construction toys. However, making a robot perform those same tasks reliably in the harsh environment of space presents a far greater engineering challenge.

The team encountered technical difficulties and scheduling constraints that prevented it from finishing the entire antenna. Nevertheless, the robot successfully assembled an initial section, providing evidence that this construction method can work in orbit. Researchers believe the same basic approach could eventually support much larger frameworks carrying enormous reflective surfaces.

The orbital experiment represents the third stage of DARPA's research program. During the first two stages, Caltech researchers developed the construction concept, worked out the engineering design, and verified its operation in laboratory experiments on Earth. The team then had less than 12 months to manufacture, test, and deliver the space hardware to Momentus Inc., the company hosting the payload.

"Developing a payload of this complexity on such a short timeline was an enormous undertaking for our small team," says Pellegrino, who is also co-director of the Space Solar Power Project, which aims to harvest solar power in space and wirelessly transmit it to Earth's surface. "As we wrap up the mission, we are finally able to start thinking about the new avenues of research opened by this demonstration."

Why Scientists Want to Build Enormous Structures in Orbit

The ability to assemble large structures directly in space could transform astronomy, communications, and space based energy systems.

For example, future telescopes could use enormous reflective surfaces to collect more light and observe extremely distant objects. Similar structures could also support powerful radio antennas, allowing scientists and engineers to build communications systems much larger than those that can currently be launched.

One of the greatest obstacles is the limited room available inside a rocket's fairing, the protective enclosure that surrounds its payload during launch. No matter how ambitious a spacecraft design might be, its components must somehow fit inside that confined space.

Traditionally, engineers have addressed this problem in two ways. They either fold large structures into compact packages that can unfold after reaching orbit, or they launch separate components and have astronauts assemble them in space. Both approaches impose practical limits on the size and complexity of the finished structure.

Robotic construction offers a third possibility. Instead of fitting an enormous telescope or antenna inside a rocket, engineers could transport its materials into orbit and assemble the complete system there.

DARPA's Plan for Kilometer-Scale Space Structures

DARPA established NOM4D in 2022 to investigate technologies that could eventually "ferry raw materials from Earth for in-orbit manufacturing," according to the program's website.

Caltech's ASTRA experiment is one of only two projects selected to advance to the program's third phase, which involves demonstrating construction technologies in orbit.

The other project, led by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, will use a module attached to the International Space Station to investigate a technique for hardening carbon tubes in space. This could provide another way to manufacture structural components without having to complete every step on Earth.

"NOM4D's objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space," said Andrew Detor, DARPA program manager for NOM4D, in a written statement. "By 'very large,' I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today."

Such structures could eventually be several football fields long or even extend for kilometers, far beyond the dimensions of conventional spacecraft.

How Caltech's Construction Robot Reached Space

ASTRA began its journey on March 30, 2026, when a SpaceX Transporter-16 mission launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California early that morning.

The robot traveled aboard Momentus Inc.'s Vigoride 7 orbital vehicle, which carried 10 separate payloads into low Earth orbit. ASTRA occupied approximately one cubic meter of space, a compact package containing both the assembly machinery and the materials required for construction.

Inside were two previously assembled truss bays, reinforced with diagonal tubes and connecting joints. The payload also included a robotic arm and motorized dispensers loaded with the parts needed to construct the remaining sections.

The successful launch was an emotional moment for the small engineering team watching from Earth. Jaden Suh, a former Caltech postdoctoral scholar who is now an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin, was moved to tears as the spacecraft carrying his team's work headed into orbit.

"As a child, I was super curious about and interested in space structures. Just like many other engineers working in this field, sending your stuff to space is what I've been dreaming of my entire life," Suh says. "I was extremely lucky to have the opportunity to work on this project, beginning from scratch. A lot of my original ideas are included in this system, and it was just incredible seeing it reach space."

Building a Structure Hundreds of Miles Above Earth

After ASTRA reached orbit, researchers began operating the system by transmitting instructions to its onboard computer through the Vigoride spacecraft.

The initial steps involved releasing the mechanisms that had secured the components during launch. The robot then extended the two previously assembled truss bays out of the machine and proceeded to construct a third bay using the onboard assembly system.

Three team members managed the construction commands from Earth: Charles Sommer, a former Caltech systems engineer; Alan Truong, a Caltech research engineer; and graduate student Tara Venkatadri (MS '24).

Although the robot carried out the assembly operations automatically, the researchers monitored its progress using photographs transmitted from orbit. When something went wrong, they examined the images, adjusted their instructions, and attempted the operation again.

These setbacks were an important part of learning whether the technology could function outside a controlled laboratory.

"That's basically the reason you do proof-of-concept testing. There are a lot of differences in the space environment compared to down on Earth," Suh explains. "There are always lots of little surprises."

To diagnose problems in orbit, the engineers relied on a second ASTRA system kept at Pellegrino's laboratory at Caltech. This backup unit, known as a flight spare, allowed researchers to recreate difficulties encountered by the spaceborne robot and experiment with possible solutions.

"Every time we confirm there is an issue in space, we come to the laboratory and try to mimic the problem on the ground," Sommer says.

Communication restrictions made troubleshooting especially challenging. The team could contact ASTRA only during approximately seven or eight brief periods each day, with each opportunity lasting about 15 minutes.

That meant engineers had to make the most of their limited communication windows. They used the laboratory twin to investigate problems, evaluate different solutions, and determine which adjustments were most likely to work. Once a solution was ready, they sent the revised instructions to the robot in orbit.

This process helped the team work through numerous unexpected difficulties while gathering valuable information about what future autonomous construction systems will need to operate more reliably.

ASTRA's intended construction process involves repeating a carefully coordinated series of movements.

First, the robotic arm retrieves structural components from their storage dispensers. It positions the tubes and joints on an assembly plate and connects them to create a new truss bay.

Once the framework is assembled, the robot is designed to attach a thin reflective film containing many tiny openings. This material forms two reflective cable nets that are held under tension against one another by springs, helping the resulting surface maintain its intended shape.

The special film was jointly invented by researchers at Caltech and the University of Pennsylvania, where the collaborating team was led by Professor Igor Bargatin.

Unlike the knitted metallic mesh typically used in reflectors designed to fold and unfold, the perforated film requires less tension to maintain its shape. That allows engineers to reduce the amount of supporting structure needed, potentially making the entire assembly substantially lighter.

Lower weight is especially valuable in space engineering because every additional kilogram increases the demands placed on a launch vehicle.

When a bay is finished and its reflective components have been prepared, the robotic system pushes the completed section outward into space. It then begins assembling the next bay.

The full ASTRA antenna design calls for 11 connected bays, each attached to the reflective nets and extended outward from the assembly system.

A Small Demonstration With Enormous Implications

Despite successfully demonstrating the construction technique, the researchers do not expect ASTRA to finish assembling all 11 bays before the mission concludes in December.

The experiment has revealed several ways the robotic hardware and assembly procedure could be simplified and improved. Even without a completed antenna, the team believes it has collected enough evidence to establish that the approach is technically feasible.

The implications extend well beyond the relatively small antenna used in this demonstration.

Future robotic construction systems could help scientists build gigantic space telescopes that collect more light, radio antennas capable of supporting advanced communications, and enormous solar arrays designed to capture sunlight in orbit.

Such solar power systems could potentially transmit collected energy wirelessly to receivers on Earth, an idea being explored through Caltech's Space Solar Power Project.

More broadly, the successful test suggests that the size of future space infrastructure may not always have to be dictated by the dimensions of the rockets used to launch its components.

"Once you get to the size limit where structures cannot be prebuilt on the ground and unfolded, you have to think about how to build them in space," Pellegrino says. "So, this work could be useful not only for astronomy and astrophysics but also for communications and other areas, such as building very large solar arrays for space solar power."

#4327. The highly-anticipated follow-up to Baldur's Gate 3 is more Divinity, but it's not technically Original Sin 3

Larian has returned to tease a grand vision for its next major project, a new Divinity.

Larian Studios has delivered what was arguably the biggest reveal of The Game Awards 2025 showcase. The Hellstone, the mysterious monolith in the desert that’s been generating a lot of speculation in the lead-up to the show was indeed teasing the studio’s next game.

The Belgian developer is returning to the series it created with Divinity, a non-numbered sequel that’s designed for new and veteran players alike. The announcement was entirely cinematic, setting the tone for what looks to be the next big thing in the space.

Larian calls Divinity its most ambitious title ever, with the studio striving for a level of depth and breadth we’ve not seen before. This is the next project from the Baldur’s Gate 3 team, after all, so there’s understandably immense anticipation for it.

Divinity is a standalone RPG, and does not require you to have played Divinity: Original Sin, or Divinity: Original Sin 2. If you did, however, you’re going to find the journey extra special because of the continuity it offers.

“We’re ready to bring everything we’ve done previously into one place,” said founder and game director, Swen Vincke.

“This marks the beginning of something with more breadth, depth, and intimacy than anything we’ve created before. We’ve been building toward this moment ever since we took our fate into our own hands. This is the Divinity we’ve always wanted to make and you're going to have loads of fun with it.”

Beyond that, there’s precious little that’s been revealed for Divinity so far. We don’t know what platforms it’s going to be coming to, nor do we even have a release target. We do know it’s an RPG, so you can very much expect something similar to earlier games in the series, and, of course, Baldur’s Gate 3.

#4326. Arc Raiders' Cold Snap update brings snow storms to most maps, new events and a new Raider Deck

Arc Raiders has delivered a big new update that's very fittingly on theme, and it's not without new mechanics.

Arc Raiders is kicking off its last major event of the year. The Cold Snap update arrives moments from now, and it’s perhaps the game’s biggest since its momentous launch in late October. We’ve known about the existence of Cold Snap for a while, of course, but we finally have a solid idea about what to expect.

Cold Snap is made up of different components - including new content - that all players have access to.

As the name suggests, of course, Cold Snap introduces the new snowfall Map Condition. As part of this, maps will be covered in snow, thanks to snowstorms sweeping across them. For one, snowfall makes it harder to see enemies, but it also turns all lakes solid.

There’s a new mechanic associated with this, and it’s actually similar to Battlefield 6’s Winter Offensive update. Staying outdoors for too long will cause you to catch frostbite, which slowly drains HP. Embark says you’re going to need to bring more healing items with you on raids, and it doesn’t look like there are firepits that could keep you warm - though staying indoors for a while will help.

Cold Snap arrives alongside limited-time events that will be available until Tuesday, January 13. The snowfall visual update and new frostbite mechanics are available on Dam Battlegrounds, Buried City, Spaceport, and The Blue Gate.

One of the new events is Flickering Flames, which comes with its own progression track of 25 levels. Content is, of course, unlocked using Merits, which are earned from XP in matches. The other event is the Candleberry Banquet Project, which requires you to donate items found on the surface (including Candleberries).

You’ll earn rewards each time, and each stage completed will reveal a new scene on the banquet table. Likewise, there are cosmetic rewards as part of each stage, and you can use it as a source of Merits, too.

While on the subject, the new update also kicks off a new Raider Deck (battle pass). Available from December 26, The Goalie Raider Deck is pretty much what you’d expect. You’ll find several pages of cosmetic and useful items. The new Deck will be available to all players for free.

#4325. Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising new approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

The findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis

At the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored."

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis

The researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

When the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

This connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

The team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang says.

Common Supplement Shows Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases."

Against world No.1 FURIA on Wednesday, The MongolZ recovered after dropping the opening map. MOUZ have also booked a semi-final place after going unbeaten in Group B.

The defeat ended a seven-game winning run for FURIA, HLTV said, although the match was not an elimination game. FURIA had not lost since winning PGL Masters Bucharest. They now face BetBoom in the quarter-finals.

The second map, Cache, was FURIA’s own pick, and The MongolZ had lost on that map in each of their previous four attempts. This time they won it, then closed out the series on the third map.

The timing gives the result extra weight. IEM Beijing is ESL’s top-tier CS2 event and the last big tournament before the Major. FURIA are still alive, but the series shows they can be beaten by the sides around them.

Falcons went out in the Group A lower-bracket final. NAVI recovered from a narrow loss on the opening map and dominated the rest of the series. On the Mirage decider, NAVI won all 12 rounds of their T-side half.

w0nderful went 25-4 on Inferno. b1t then took over on Mirage.

#4323. 10 Metroidvanias With the Most Nominations at The Game Awards

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Although Metroidvanias have been largely dominated by indie games since video game award ceremonies became commonplace, this hasn't diminished their presence at the industry's most important gala events.

Today, the indie ecosystem is just as capable as AAA titles of delivering masterpieces, which has led to them gaining a more prominent role whenever we gather to review each year's best releases.

Certainly, it's not as prominent a genre as RPGs or pure action-adventure games, but it has still had enough presence to demonstrate that it's a variant that has nothing to envy in the legitimacy of others.

Therefore, clarifying beforehand that several titles will be omitted for sharing the last spot with only one nomination, prioritizing instead those that were most relevant, these are the ten Metroidvanias with the most nominations at The Game Awards.

Along with another title that will be featured later, Axiom Verge marks the first year a Metroidvania earned a nomination; in this case, for Best Independent Game of 2015.

Although it had to contend with notable releases like the global phenomenon Rocket League and the indie gem Undertale, Tom Happ secured his place in the genre's history thanks to his magnificent science fiction journey.

In an era when Metroidvanias hadn't yet established themselves as a major force, this solo developer created such a captivating title that, to this day, it still has few direct competitors in its craftsmanship, as it is truly unique.

Nothing would please me more today than an Axiom Verge 3, so this is a fitting opportunity to recall the historic feat achieved by the first entry and ask Happ to consider repeating that glory soon.

As a living legend of contemporary Metroidvanias, single-handedly setting the course for the genre in the decade following its release, Hollow Knight couldn't be left off this list.

However, contrary to what one might think today, Team Cherry's creation only received a nomination for Best Indie Debut in 2017, which it lost to a colossus that, upon its release, made a greater impact: Cuphead.

Even so, time would gradually vindicate this masterpiece, whose aura would extend to all subsequent developments, rewriting history in the memories of many who recall, albeit mistakenly, that it was nominated in more categories.

The power of hindsight is undeniable when the subject is a title with Hollow Knight's legacy, which also highlights how indie games, over the years, have become increasingly respected and taken seriously in these spaces.

From indies to multiplayers, these ten video games that defined the 2010s shaped the industry as we know it today.

Leaving aside the inevitable debate about Dead Cells as a Metroidvania, Motion Twin made history by being one of the first games in the genre to receive multiple nominations at The Game Awards.

Historically, this fusion of the genre with the roguelike philosophy earned the second Metroidvania award in the event's history by winning Best Action Game in 2018, though it lost the Best Independent Game category to the acclaimed Celeste.

In the category it won, it faced stiff competition from titanic blockbusters like Call of Duty: Black Ops 4, Destiny 2: Forsaken, and Far Cry 5, though this didn't prevent what would eventually become one of the best-selling indie games of all time from taking home the prize.

The recognition is, of course, more than deserved, given that few titles in the last decade are capable of generating the excitement and addictiveness that Dead Cells produces, so no matter how many AAA games they had put against it, it would have won anyway.

That high-caliber developers like Ubisoft are investing in the genre to revitalize their longest-running franchises is a relatively new trend, yet it yielded definitive results with Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown.

The presence of a game in the genre with such a strong production value allowed it to win an unprecedented honor for Metroidvanias, the Innovation in Accessibility Award in 2024, although it lost the Best Action-Adventure Game category to Astro Bot.

Regardless, it was the first medal at The Game Awards that the French developer received after winning Best Sim/Strategy Game with Mario + Rabbids: Sparks of Hope in 2022, making its impact in terms of recognition significant.

Furthermore, it's an extraordinary video game with a superb level of polish and freshness, so hopefully Ubisoft will recognize this trend and begin to replicate what they did with Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown with several of their most forgotten and missed IPs.

2024 was a fertile year for indie games, and although it didn't win either of the categories it was nominated for—because Balatro is larger than life—Animal Well remains in the collective imagination as an unparalleled masterpiece.

As part of the nominees for Best Independent Game and Best Indie Debut in 2024, Billy Basso stood tall with his iconic solo project against giants of the indie ecosystem like Devolver Digital, Kepler Interactive, and Annapurna Interactive without hesitation.

Basso picks up the mantle from Happ and doubles Axiom Verge's achievement almost a decade later, doing so with a game that defies Metroidvania conventions and replaces all combat with countless intricate yet wonderful puzzles that completely immerse you in the adventure.

Two years later, Animal Well remains one of my most cherished memories of the entire decade, and I think it will likely stay there for... a lifetime.

From the hops and dashes in Hollow Knight to the integral platforming of Pseudoregalia, these are 10 Metroidvanias with satisfying platforming.

The first of this list's five Metroidvanias to be nominated for three or more awards is none other than Tunic, the indie gem that swept through audiences and critics alike in 2022, establishing itself among the genre's most outstanding representatives this generation.

Unfortunately, its nominations for Best Independent Game, Best Action-Adventure Game, and Best Indie Debut in 2022 didn't result in any badges, as it was up against GOTY contenders like Stray and God of War: Ragnarök, though this only underscores its impressive quality.

That essence reminiscent of The Legend of Zelda didn't go unnoticed, and it underpinned the structure of one of recent years' most exciting and intriguing adventures, particularly because of its decision not to hold your hand and instead rely on your ability to find your way through combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving.

The fact that Tunic is the first video game from its developers is absolutely incredible, and that under said conditions it achieved three nominations on the most anticipated night in the video game industry is quite high recognition.

As one of the most exquisite audiovisual expressions the genre has witnessed since its inception, Ori and the Will of the Wisps was an inevitable presence on any list of this caliber.

Moon Studios' sequel was among the nominees for Best Art Direction, Best Music, and Best Action-Adventure Game in 2020, though unfortunately, it had to compete against absolute generational masterpieces like Ghost of Tsushima, Final Fantasy VII Remake, and The Last of Us Part II.

However, as with Tunic, Ori and the Will of the Wisps being considered alongside numerous video games that have defined the decade is one of the greatest displays of Metroidvania greatness on the big stage.

It's no wonder the title consistently appears on lists of the best of its kind, and one that would have completely swept its categories had it been nominated in years less dominated by modern classics.

Metroid Dread made history as the first Metroidvania to be nominated for Game of the Year in 2021, and for many it was the true winner of the category that, ultimately, went to It Takes Two.

Regardless of the debate, MercurySteam solidified its relationship with Nintendo by bringing Samus Aran back to 2D, reinforcing it as the natural home of the iconic bounty hunter by delivering a near-perfect creation.

It was also nominated for Best Action-Adventure Game, which it won, and for Players’ Voice, which it lost, thus becoming the second game in the genre to win a category after Dead Cells, despite probably deserving more.

The mother of all the entries on this list is an inseparable part of its history, and although perhaps not to the fullest extent, its participation in The Game Awards is a recognition of that legacy.

From the ever-challenging Celeste to some surprisingly difficult gems, these are the 10 Hardest Indie Games To 100% Complete.

With four nominations and one victory, Ori and the Blind Forest is pure Metroidvania history, bursting onto the scene at the interactive industry's most prestigious awards ceremony as the genre's first appearance (alongside Axiom Verge).

Developed by a much smaller team than when they collaborated with Microsoft on the sequel, and as a less experienced studio within a still largely unexplored genre, the project was nominated for Best Independent Game, Best Art Direction, Best Score, and Best Action-Adventure in 2015.

Of all the nominations, it took home the award for its visual direction, beating out Bloodborne, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, and Metal Gear Solid 5: The Phantom Pain, one of the biggest surprises the ceremony has ever seen.

While this is a more common and normal occurrence these days, the fact that Ori and the Blind Forest achieved such a strong presence, and even managed to win an award among a couple of candidates for best game of all time, is simply beyond belief.

What I consider the best Metroidvania of all time is also the most recognized game in the genre at The Game Awards, leaving Hollow Knight: Silksong with the most nominations at six, though it only managed one win.

Game of the Year, Best Art Direction, Best Score and Music, Best Independent Game, Players’ Voice, and Best Action-Adventure Game were the categories in which Team Cherry's unimaginable sequel was nominated, ultimately taking home the last one.

Like Ori and the Blind Forest, Hornet had to overcome giants such as Death Stranding 2: On the Beach, Ghost of Yotei, and Split Fiction to win the award, a remarkable achievement considering the team is still just three people.

In the categories it didn't win, it was surpassed by the now-legendary Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, which took home four of the six awards in which it shared nominations, and Wuthering Waves, which won the user vote.

In any case, Hollow Knight: Silksong is the Metroidvania with the most nominations at The Game Awards, and it's tough to imagine when we'll see another title that can match such a record.

From classics like Teslagrad to modern gems like Blasphemous, these are ten Metroidvania franchises that should come back in 2027.

#4322. Arc Raiders' latest patch adds two of the most requested features, but kills Cred hoarding

The last major Arc Raiders update of the year has arrived, bringing several big new features to the game, but not without some bad news.

Embark has just rolled out patch 1.7.0 for Arc Raiders players everywhere. This is a significant patch for the extraction shooter for a number of reasons, not least of which because it kicks off a series of events under the Cold Snap banner, which introduces a new conditions to the game’s maps.

Dig deeper into the patch notes, however, and you’ll find even more to get excited about, including features players have been asking for since the game’s first public test.

To start with, today’s update finally adds an option toggle aiming down sights. This is especially relevant for PC players, most of whom play shooters with an ADS toggle, rather than hold. Another often requested feature has been the ability to reset the game’s skill tree.

This is now available for the cost of 2,000 Coins per skill point. It goes without saying that you’re going to need a whole lot of money to reset the entire thing, but it’s a useful option to have when you want to alter your path.

The next change is one that’s going to ruffle a lot of feathers. Arc Raiders now has a soft Cred cap of 800. This is now clearly shown on your Wallet screen, and the developer said the cap is necessary to prevent players from using their accumulated Cred to unlock new Raider Decks immediately after release.

The good news is that this won’t affect the Cred you may already have, but going forward, 800 is the most you can hold at any point. You’ll also notice that Shani has more stuff for you to buy with Cred, in case you want another way to spend what you have.

Patch 1.7.0 also brings a few other additions - and makes some changes - that are worth highlighting. You can now customise your Raider Tool, which likely means we’re going to see Raider Tool cosmetics going forward.

Speaking of items, the Aphelion weapon blueprint has been moved to Stella Montis, so you won’t be able to get it from taking down the Matriarch. The Bettina, and Rattler have both seen some balance changes.

The Bettina’s durability will now degrade a lot slower per shot, making it take 26 magazines to fully deplete durability. The base magazine size has been increased to 22, and the reload time has been cut to 4.5 seconds. Embark says this should make the weapon more viable in PvP, while also allowing it to stand on its own without the need for players bring a secondary weapon.

As for the Rattler, the only change it gets is an increase to its magazine size from 10 to 12. The idea is to make it about as effective as a Stitcher or Kettle at close ranges when it comes to PvP encounters.

And, of course, it wouldn’t be a big Arc Raiders patch without some tweaks to the game’s Arc enemies. This time, the Shredder gets all the love. The menacing unit now moves faster, turns more sharply and doesn’t get knocked back as much when shot.

The Shredder’s head now has more health, too, meaning you won’t be able to shoot it off early and confuse it. In general, the Arc unit should be smarter, especially when navigating narrow spaces. Finally, the Shredder now activates faster upon detecting (and being attacked by) players.

Beyond that, the main menu has seen a few changes to highlight ongoing events, make certain announcements quieter, make it easier to track Raider Quests and more. There’s a lot more in this update, too, such as changes to footstep loudness, several tweaks to loot and the value of certain items, and more besides. You’ll find the full change log on the official website.

#4321. Japanese Military Unleashes Beautiful Ace Combat 8 Recruitment Video

Bandai Namco has been basking in the glory of Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve since it came out to rave reviews on October 1, but the gaming world isn’t the only one to take advantage of the stunning tunes put together by composer Keiki Kobayashi for Project Aces’ latest game.

To celebrate the popularity of the game and the aviators that inspired it, the Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) put together a full music video scored to the Ace Combat 8 main theme, Everflow:

The video combines footage from the Japanese military’s air arm in all of its facets, including the JASDF Music Corps, which contributed to the song’s recording.

The liberal application of sick footage of fighter jets and stylish crews for propaganda and military recruitment purposes is nothing new, and nobody did it better than director Tony Scott, Tom Cruise and co. in the homoerotic naval aviation hit, Top Gun (1986).

Although the JASDF’s own attempt to leverage Ace Combat 8 into a recruitment drive is a lot more subtle, it does a brilliant job showcasing the different specialties and career paths available to prospective airmen

Seven years after Ace Combat 7, Wings of Theve is already number one on Steam and the second highest rated entry in the franchise's history.

Ace Combat 8 fans will recognize the F-15J and F-2A fighters from the game’s tech tree.

The F-15J is a domestically produced variant of the McDonnell Douglas (now Boeing) F-15C Eagle air superiority fighter. Built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries from 1980 to 1999, the fleet has been heavily upgraded throughout its life, effectively becoming a multirole fighter.

In Ace Combat 8, the F-15J is the only aircraft of Western design to carry the High-Power Air-to-Air Missile (HPAA) special weapon. It’s a poor weapon against maneuvering targets like fighters, but you can send a whole generation of Sotoan bomber pilots to an early grave with these.

The video combines footage from the Japanese military’s air arm in all of its facets, including the JASDF Music Corps

Also built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries is the F-2A, nicknamed ‘Viper Zero’ as a tribute to the F-16 it is derived from and Mitsubishi’s A6M Zero of World War 2 fame. The F-2A is a heavier, larger evolution of the F-16 design, and holds the distinction of being the first-ever fighter to have an AESA radar. As in real life, its Ace Combat 8 counterpart differs from the F-16C through the ability to fire long-range anti-ship missiles (LASM).

Although the F-35A and F-35B feature in the video, Ace Combat 8 only has the F-35C naval version, which makes sense given the FCU Endurance is factually a protagonist in the game. The aircraft represents the late-game pick in the multirole tech tree on the Western side, with the F-22A holding up the air-to-air side.

Another nice touch from the JASDF is the presentation of certain squadrons depicted in Ace Combat 8 style, with badges and an aura-farming shot of the aircraft before all hell breaks loose.

Ace Combat is no stranger to collaborating with the Japanese military. In 2021, Bandai Namco released a Japan Air Self-Defense Force DLC for Ace Combat 7: Skies Unknown that added real JASDF liveries to the aircraft in-game and brought back a series of bangers from the franchise’s previous soundtrack.

Since the turn of the century, Japanese military recruitment has stood out against many of its Western peers for how it tries to leverage pop culture, including video games and anime (a whole lot of it), to engage with its target audience, instead of testosterone-infused montages or melodramatic beach volleyball shots.

The Japanese military made headlines back in 2015 with its collaboration with the GATE series, an Isekai manga (later anime) based on the Japan Self-Defense Forces fighting in a fantasy world.

Perhaps the most famous crossover of anime and aircraft in the land is the ‘Kisarazu Sisters’. Between 2011 and 2013, four AH-1S Cobra attack helicopters based in Kisarazu, Chiba Prefecture, got commemorative paint jobs with original anime-style characters designed at the 4th Anti-Tank Helicopter Unit. They were immortalized in the game world through War Thunder, with the AH-1S Kisarazu premium vehicle.

The success of these JSDF recruitment drives is outside the scope of video game coverage, but as an Ace Combat fan, I can only hope they keep making great videos like this.

#4320. It’s official: Battlefield 6 is 2025's best-selling game, but Black Ops 7 still managed to be November’s top-seller

2025 will be remembered for many things, but in the ultra-competitive games industry, it’s going to be thought of as the year Battlefield 6 did what many thought couldn’t happen.

Circan’s November 2025 video game sales report has easily been one of the most anticipated. For one, November is always one of the most lucrative for the games industry, but this year in particular has seen several major hits - including new entries in two rival series.

We’re talking, of course, about Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 the latest releases in their respective multiplayer shooter series. The decades-old fight to claim the top spot has long been won by Call of Duty, but the latest Battlefield has achieved what many thought was impossible.

Cricana’s report covers spending on video game software, hardware, and accessories in the U.S. November 2025 saw spending fall by 4% compared to November 2024, bringing in a total of $5.9 billion.

Software technically saw growth during the month, but declines in hardware, and accessories were mainly responsible for the drop in overall spending. Black Ops 7 continued Call of Duty’s 18-Year Streak in topping sales in its launch month.

However, this year’s game did not also top the year-to-date charts, something the series has done consistently, and more than any other top-selling game each year - with rare exceptions. Battlefield 6 is firmly in the lead there, cementing its claim as 2025’s best-selling title. Black Ops 7, fittingly, occupies in the #7 spot there.

Separately from the best-selling game title fight, November has actually been one of the worst for the industry in terms of hardware sales. The report notes that the three major platform holders - Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo have all seen their hardware sales decline.

Spending on hardware during November amounted to only $695 million, a massive 27% decline compared to November 2024. According to the report, that’s the worst dollar amount total for any November since 2005, when it comes to hardware specifically. All three current-gen consoles totaled 1.6 million units sold, which Circana also notes is the lowest for any November since 1995.

This all doesn’t bode especially well for the industry. November has always been a key holiday shopping month, but it’s clear the constantly rising console prices - and already high game prices - have had a big impact.

#4317. Zelda: Ocarina of Time Review: A Modern Remake With an Old Soul

Nintendo brings one of gaming's most influential adventures into the modern era without losing the magic that made it special.

I don't think I'll ever forget the first time I played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Not because I remember every detail of that first adventure, but because it was literally the first video game I ever played.

I was just a little kid who barely understood English, sitting in front of a Nintendo 64 with a controller (which, yes, wasn't even connected to the console because I was the younger sister) and a dictionary by my side. I had no idea what half the characters were saying, but I knew I wanted to see what happened next. Nearly 30 years later, I find myself returning to that same adventure, this time with a much better understanding of English and a controller that actually works. And, surprisingly enough, I think this might be one of the most emotionally powerful experiences I've had with a remake in a long time.

From Darksiders to Shinobi: Art of Vengeance, I present to you ten action-adventure games that are unexpected masterpieces.

Sure, we all know how revolutionary Ocarina of Time was back in 1998. Its approach to 3D level design, exploration, combat, and storytelling helped shape the entire industry, establishing a reference that countless games would follow for decades. But this remake doesn't seem interested in proving that all over again.

So, rather than trying to reinvent one of gaming's most influential adventures, Nintendo seems much more interested in touching something deeper than any groundbreaking mechanic ever could: the memories we built with this little boy, his fairy, and a world that once felt impossibly big.

For starters, let's get one thing out of the way: despite Nintendo's pre-release marketing describing this as a ground-up remake a few times, don't expect something along the lines of Square Enix's Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy. This is actually a faithful recreation of the original, much closer in spirit to what Nintendo did with Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask on the Nintendo 3DS.

The main story remains practically untouched, the overall structure is familiar, and most of the changes come in the form of visual improvements, quality-of-life adjustments, and a handful of additions that make the experience feel more modern. This means that if you've played the original, you'll recognize almost everything here.

And I can understand that this might disappoint some people. When a remake is announced as being built from the ground up, it's natural to expect substantial changes, perhaps even a new interpretation of familiar locations, mechanics, or story moments. But I think it all comes down to what you expect from this particular adventure in the end.

If you've played the original, you'll recognize almost everything here.

As a longtime Zelda fan who literally learned how to play video games with Link, I found this approach much more effective than I initially imagined, since it allowed the remake to strike a point much deeper than any new fancy level design could ever reach, largely because it understands that Ocarina of Time doesn't need a completely different story to make us feel something all over again.

Instead, it gives us that very same story with a series of carefully considered tweaks. Some are immediately noticeable, while others are the kind of little details you might not even realize have changed until you've spent a few hours exploring Hyrule again. And there's no better place to start discussing these changes than with the story itself.

If you've somehow never experienced Ocarina of Time, here's the short version: you're a little boy without a fairy who happens to oversleep one morning, only to be awakened by a very concerned fairy named Navi. Before long, you're thrown into a journey to save the world, involving a mysterious princess and an evil Gerudo king.

It's a wonderfully straightforward premise that gradually evolves into something much bigger, exploring themes of childhood, growing up, loss, and how the passage of time feels bittersweet for us all. And, nearly three decades later, its emotional impact remains remarkably intact. However, the remake introduces something that makes these familiar moments feel considerably more powerful: dedicated cutscenes with voice acting.

The original Ocarina of Time did an incredible job with the hardware limitations of the Nintendo 64. Seriously, the developers managed to create some wonderfully expressive moments with not much to work with back then. But now, these scenes finally have the cinematic presentation they've always deserved – and boy, does it make a difference!

I honestly lost count of how many times I caught myself wearing the dumbest smile while watching a cutscene. Seeing Princess Ruto slowly abandon her grumpy attitude as she falls for Link, watching Darunia dance to Saria's Song as if he's attending the greatest concert of his life, or witnessing the moment we realize Ganondorf only managed to obtain the power he wanted because we essentially fell for his little scheme.

These scenes have so much more personality now, and the voice performances help give familiar characters a newfound sense of life. More importantly, they made me realize something rather unexpected: deep down, these were already the scenes I had imagined back in 1998. As a child, we had essentially created a full version of these moments in our heads, but the remake gave those childhood interpretations a proper visual and emotional form, and that's a pretty wonderful achievement!

More importantly, they made me realize something rather unexpected: deep down, these were already the scenes I had imagined back in 1998.

And speaking of giving familiar characters more room to breathe, there's another storytelling improvement here that I absolutely love: how NPCs are way more important now.

The remake's dev team included younger folks, several of whom never played the original Ocarina of Time, who provided a much-needed modern view of things.

One of my favorite things about Ocarina of Time has always been its worldbuilding. Hyrule is filled with strange, charming, and occasionally downright questionable people, each with their own little stories and quirks. But the remake takes this aspect of the original and expands it in a surprisingly meaningful way.

Here's a tiny detail that makes a huge difference around here: time now passes continuously within Hyrule's towns. Basically, in the original, the world essentially had four different environmental states: Child Link during the day and night, and Adult Link during the day and night. This allowed certain characters and events to appear depending on the time period and Link's age, but the system was somewhat restrictive because time wouldn't actually progress while you were exploring towns.

Now, the remake changes that! The sun rises and sets naturally as you explore even inside cities, with characters appearing and disappearing according to their own schedules (except in more contained areas such as temples and minigame shops).

It's a small adjustment that makes the towns feel much more organic, almost as if their inhabitants finally have their own agendas, which gives it a lovely Majora’s Mask vibe. Also, this adds additional events and dialogue associated with these new day-night cycles, giving us more opportunities to learn about people we previously knew very little about.

My favorite example of this is Grog, who is arguably one of the saddest characters in the entire game. Remember that punk-looking guy who sits beneath a tree in Kakariko Village at night, complaining that everyone he knows is disgusting? In the original, we only really encounter him twice: once as Child Link and later in the Lost Woods as Adult Link. Well, thanks to the new time system, you can now find him walking around Kakariko Village during the day, too. And he has more dialogue and new interactions, finally giving more weight to fan theories that have circulated about him for nearly 30 years!

And this isn’t an isolated example. Several other characters receive similar attention, making Hyrule feel like a much more interconnected place. I absolutely love this kind of addition because it doesn't just give us more content for the sake of having more content. It actually enriches a world we already know, rewards longtime fans who have spent years discussing its little mysteries, and makes its characters feel like actual inhabitants rather than people waiting for Link to show up. It just makes everything feel a little more real.

Okay, so the remake has the storytelling side covered. But what about the actual gameplay? After all, Ocarina of Time wouldn't have become such an influential title without its approach to exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving.

The good news is that the core experience remains remarkably faithful, although there are plenty of quality-of-life improvements that make returning to Hyrule considerably more comfortable.

For starters, the item menu has been reduced to three main tabs, with a much cleaner organization that makes finding and equipping things considerably easier. I have to admit that I wasn't particularly fond of the menu taking direct inspiration from Breath of the Wild, since different games have very different needs. However, the new quick-access carousel is an absolute lifesaver, and switching between items during exploration and combat feels much more fluid. You no longer have to spend quite so much time navigating menus just to equip something.

And there's also a second quick-access system dedicated to some of your most essential tools, including the Ocarina, Lens of Truth, Happy Mask Salesman's masks, and (yes, you can finally celebrate!) the Iron Boots. This last addition is particularly welcome because it addresses one of the most infamous frustrations of the original game: the Water Temple.

But don't think everything is perfect just because most changes are improvements. Some of the modernized design decisions have introduced a few restrictions that, to be completely honest, I'm not entirely convinced were necessary. For instance, certain pieces of equipment have been tweaked to prevent players from using them in ways the developers seemingly never intended.

This happened with the Hookshot, which was previously a wonderful tool for experimenting with different traversal possibilities, but now only attaches to specific designated surfaces. That means you can no longer use it to reach rooftops, for example. Does this force you to find alternative solutions? Sure. But it also takes away some of the creativity and freedom that made experimenting with the original game's mechanics so much fun.

Still, this is where expectations come into play again. And there is something important to highlight: overall, the remake makes your life considerably easier than it was back in 1998, which means that finding new solutions isn’t actually hard. Around here, NPCs offer more hints and several sequences have been optimized to deliver a more straightforward experience. Oh, and there's also a dedicated quest log that helps you keep track of both the main adventure and your secondary objectives.

While I wasn't particularly happy about the Hookshot changes, I never felt like they significantly compromised my experience. Finding alternative solutions was generally okay, and the improvements elsewhere made the overall gameplay feel much smoother. So it's a trade-off, and one that I think works more often than it doesn't.

Eiji Aonuma and the development team for the Ocarina of Time remake discussed how one of the original's infamous dungeons is being improved.

Now, here's where things get a little more complicated. As you might expect from a remake that's practically a 1:1 recreation, exploration remains very faithful to the original. And while the quality-of-life improvements make moving around Hyrule much more pleasant, they don't necessarily change how you interact with the world itself.

There are some additional visual indicators to help you find interesting things, though. Poes in Hyrule Field are now associated with specific fences, and Lake Hylia is no longer “separated” from the field, for example, making some environmental details easier to identify locations worth investigating. But the overall level design is pretty much what we experienced back in 1998, for better or worse.

And I have mixed feelings about that. On one hand, revisiting these locations with modernized controls and an entirely new visual presentation is an incredibly emotional experience. I genuinely enjoyed wandering around places I hadn't seen in years, recognizing familiar spots, and discovering little details that I had completely forgotten about. It's the kind of experience that makes you want to stop every few minutes just to appreciate how much care went into recreating this world.

On the other hand, I can't help wondering whether the developers could have gone a little further, especially since Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom have completely changed our expectations of what exploring Hyrule can mean, giving us approximately 984,396 things to discover while traveling from point A to point B. Compared to those experiences, Ocarina of Time's more structured approach can feel a little restrictive, particularly when you know exactly where everything is supposed to be.

I would have loved to see a few more surprises along the way, perhaps additional secrets or expanded areas that rewarded players for approaching familiar locations from a different perspective. But, once again, I need to consider what this remake is trying to accomplish. As someone with an almost unhealthy amount of nostalgia running through my veins, I honestly didn't mind revisiting a place I consider home, even if the journey remained largely unchanged! However, if you're expecting a completely redesigned Hyrule with new exploration mechanics and substantially expanded areas, I'd recommend keeping those expectations in check.

Now, let's talk about the elephant in the room: the visuals. The remake retains the colorful, whimsical identity of the original, but practically everything has been reimagined from an aesthetic standpoint. Hyrule now looks even more like a fantasy world, with lush environments, intricate textures, expressive character models, and an almost overwhelming amount of environmental detail.

I have to confess that the new art direction took some getting used to. Kokiri Forest, in particular, initially felt a little too dense for my taste. Come on, don't any of these Kokiri kids own a lawn mower? And Young Link's redesigned appearance also gave me some mixed feelings during my first few hours.

But the more I played, the more the new aesthetic grew on me. Before I knew it, I was completely obsessed with how beautiful everything looked. And a big part of that comes down to the character designs. Rather than simply updating existing models with higher-resolution textures, the developers have reimagined several characters and enemies to better fit the remake's more elaborate fantasy aesthetic. The result feels cohesive, and there's a clear sense of inspiration behind practically every design.

Not to mention the little details! You can see (and feel, since this game is all about feelings, right?) just how much attention went into recreating familiar locations. Kakariko Village's well, for example, now features carefully rendered water and a variety of textures that make the environment feel considerably more tangible. Even something as simple as watching Link play the Ocarina becomes a visual treat, since you can actually see his fingers moving to the correct notes.

Also, the developers clearly know which details longtime fans care about. One particularly memorable example is how they've handled one of the game's most terrifying creatures (you know who!), since it is scarier than ever. And several bosses have also received additional visual details and updated animations that make their encounters feel more imposing.

And it's these little touches that make the difference! The remake doesn't just want Hyrule to look prettier; it wants every familiar corner to feel worth revisiting. And, honestly, I could spend hours just walking around and appreciating it all.

Putting everything together, I think it's fair to say that this is a remake that successfully modernizes a classic without losing its old soul. And considering how heavily nostalgia has influenced the gaming industry lately, with remakes and remasters seemingly arriving every other month, it's nice to see one that understands exactly what made its source material so special.

Most of the improvements are welcome, even if a few decisions (sorry, I still won't forgive what happened to the Hookshot) leave something to be desired. The updated gameplay makes the experience feel much more accessible, the visual overhaul is gradually gorgeous, and the additional storytelling touches give familiar characters a newfound sense of personality.

Putting everything together, I think it's fair to say that this is a remake that successfully modernizes a classic without losing its old soul.

There are also several additions that I’m obsessed with, from hearing iconic characters speak for the first time to seeing long-standing fan theories receive more attention, not to mention the extra Ocarina mechanics that let you hum melodies into the microphone to play them. It's a collection of thoughtful changes that, when put together, makes this adventure feel surprisingly fresh without sacrificing what made it so memorable.

And that's precisely why I think this remake works so well for longtime fans. It doesn't ask us to forget the original or replace the memories we built with it. Instead, it gives us an opportunity to experience those same feelings again, now with a presentation and gameplay that feel right at home in 2026. But I also believe it works wonderfully as an entry point for newcomers! Despite its faithful structure, the modernized controls, expanded guidance, and quality-of-life improvements make the experience feel far less dated than the original. So you can still appreciate everything that made Ocarina of Time revolutionary without having to deal with every limitation of a game released nearly three decades ago.

In the end, this remake made me feel like that little kid again, waking up early on Saturday mornings to spend hours exploring Hyrule, controller in hand (and, thankfully, connected this time). And I could feel that this was exactly what Nintendo wanted to accomplish within the first few minutes.

Playing this remake reminded me that video games can be much more than the mechanics we praise, the level design we analyze, the technical achievements we celebrate, or framerates that we fear to drop. Sometimes, their greatest power lies in how they make us feel, even decades after we've first experienced them – and Ocarina of Time still has that magic. Now, if you'll excuse me, I still have a few Golden Skulltulas and Heart Pieces to collect. And then? Well, I think I'm ready for another adventure.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games of all time, but these remakes might be just as meaningful to fans.

Sucker Punch, the team behind Ghost of Yōtei, Ghost of Tsushima, Infamous, and Sly Cooper, has been hit with layoffs, according to a report by Aftermath. The outlet states that 26 roles have been affected as the studio prepares its next project.

Aftermath cites a former Sucker Punch employee who confirmed the number of layoffs. The outlet also obtained a company email announcing the staff cuts.

“After carefully observing the challenges in the market and reviewing the team needs for our next project, we've decided to make some staffing reductions. The release coincided with the arrival of two substantial DLCs: the story expansion Echoes of Sekigahara and a roguelike mode called Most Wanted that reintroduces Ghost of Tsushima hero Jin Sakai as a playable character.
