#4312. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Goes Nuclear Against ‘Lobby Shopping’

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Players have used third-party applications to assist their play for years now, to mixed success and intent. Many benign apps for games like League and Valorant give easier access to community info, while other, more malicious cheats can completely ruin a game for everyone else in the lobby.

After unjustly banning a Battlefield 6 player, EA lost a court case to keep the ban in place.

Call of Duty: Warzone players have been utilizing one of the oddest forms of cheating I’ve ever heard of, peeking at the skill level of everyone in the lobby through the app Warzone Agent to decide whether or not to just leave the game. Activision has announced they’re clamping down hard on the practice, looking to eliminate it going forward.

Call of Duty players have been complaining about the franchise’s skill-based matchmaking (SBMM) for years now, a system where players are matched against foes equivalent to their skill level. This is, of course, how most matchmaking systems work, but COD players have been asking for its elimination since the original Modern Warfare remake.

In order to avoid these close matches, they utilize apps like Warzone Agent to figure out the average rank of the lobby before deciding to play, a practice Warzone’s anti-cheat division, Ricochet, has officially stood against. In their release surrounding the practice of lobby shopping, “moving forward, players who leave Warzone Agent loaded will not be able to access Multiplayer modes.”

Lobby shopping is the practice of hopping around warm-up stage lobbies to search for one with a lower skill ceiling, essentially targeting worse players to maximize your own boons. Activision has made it clear they won’t stand to suffer the practice any longer, further saying, “using unauthorized software to manipulate the player experience violates Activision Terms of Use and leaves your account and hardware subject to enforcement.”

Many benign apps for games like League and Valorant give easier access to community info, while other, more malicious cheats can completely ruin a game for everyone else in the lobby.

Threatening to drop the ban hammer on violators is a great way to shake the practice off, and Activision isn’t stopping there, clarifying what it considers cheating. That includes external account boosting, led by swarms of bots they’ve managed to start stomping out.

Bots plague any free-to-play game people want to put time into, and focusing more on curtailing them is a great step toward slowing the flow, even if it is just a bandage over the wound. For now, Activision has drawn their line in the sand. The only question is whether or not they’ll flinch in the face of community complaints, but they’ve stuck by their guns this long.

The community complaint around skill-based matchmaking has always struck me as incredibly odd, with these players mostly desiring a true random selection process. These random matches are, on paper, more varied, but in practice lead to matches that are total stomps for one side or the other, leaving plenty of players with a bad taste in their mouths.

Getting to be the one stomping can be great fun, but that’s also possible against players of your skill level. SBMM’s main purpose is to minimize the games that feel like complete wipes from the loser’s perspective, keeping them playing against those who are actually equivalent to them on a broad scale. It’s far from perfect, but it's better than literally just tossing a random selection of players in a room.

Without it, not only would many casual players have to gamble on getting crushed every other game, but Activision could lose those players after enough rough matches, the true reason for the practice’s continued support. Despite the complaints, Activision has clearly long since decided that skill-based matchmaking is the best middle ground for skilled and casual players alike, giving everyone designated lobbies where they’re at least promised matches that are competitive.

Modern Warfare 4's launch party is still going, with a free play period for DMZ ready to rake in new players.

#4311. Grammy Award-Winning Composer Austin Wintory Shares His Early Musical Drafts Intended For Mass Effect 5

Last week, EA shut down Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare, which resulted in the cancellation of the fifth Mass Effect game that was announced in 2020. As the fallout from this closure settles, famed video game composer Austin Wintory has shared that he'd been working on a potential soundtrack for the now-canceled game and has publicly released early versions of this score.

In a Bluesky thread, Wintory, who has composed soundtracks for games such as Journey, Sword of the Sea (for which he won a Grammy), Assassin’s Creed: Syndicate, and The Banner Saga trilogy, writes, “Mass Effect was my ultimate white whale, my all-time dream project. For the last couple years I'd been in discussion w/ BioWare & EA to take on the project & as part of that I wrote close to 20 minutes of music to explore where the franchise can go next, may as well share it!"

Wintory uploaded a 20-minute video consisting of eight tracks to his YouTube channel. The video begins with a message further elaborating on the partnership between BioWare, EA, and him. “For the past several years, I’d been in dialogue with people both at BioWare and EA to potentially jump into Mass Effect 5. As part of these conversations, I decided to surprise the team by writing/recording a gigantic love letter to the franchise, with my idea of where it can go next.”

Wintory adds that he composed the music in 2025 and that he “knew nothing” about what Mass Effect 5's story entailed when he did. As such, he describes the music as “narratively speculative.” He adds that this conceptual soundtrack was a direct homage to Jack Wall and Sam Hulick’s soundtrack on the first Mass Effect “while leaning even harder on true analog synths, and a more complex integration of the orchestra (almost akin to the hybrid nature of The Matrix),” he writes. Each music track features a message by Wintory explaining his inspiration for its production.

“Receiving the news alongside everyone else that EA had decided to not only cancel the project but shutdown BioWare entirely was a deeply felt loss," Wintory writes in the video's description. "It's been hard to see dear friends lose their jobs, and this beloved franchise seemingly vanish forever. Thank you nonetheless to everyone at BioWare and EA's music department for gifting me the chance to dream in your sandbox. It was a privilege to do even that much.”

Wintory's music is the latest piece of potential Mass Effect 5 content to emerge since BioWare’s closure. A day after the shutdown announcement, an unreleased but reportedly legitimate cinematic trailer for the canceled Mass Effect leaked online.

#4309. Legendary game creator Vince Zampella has passed away

Vince Zampella, co-creator of Call of Duty, and a veteran studio head responsible for some of the biggest franchises in the world, is gone.

Vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died. Zampella, 55, died in a car crash in Los Angeles on Sunday. The fatal crash killed him, along with the occupant of his car.

According to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles. Zampella was unfortunately trapped in an ensuing car fire, and the passenger was ejected.

Vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators. His storied career is long, and is responsible for some of the biggest shooter franchises in history. It started with Medal of Honor in the 90s, a game that changed WW2 shooters forever.

Zampella later co-founded the legendary Infinity Ward in 2002, the team that would go on to redefine multiplayer shooters forever. Infinity Ward is the studio responsible for the Call of Duty series, which remains one of the biggest games for publisher Activision, and the entire industry.

Zampella then left the studio he founded in 2010 following a major fallout with Activision. He, along with longtime collaborator, Jason West, went to rival publisher EA to form Respawn Entertainment.

Respawn went on to create the Titanfall series, and later Apex Legends. The studio is responsible for non-shooters, of course, like the third-person action game series Star Wars Jedi. Zampella was instrumental in making the game possible, having hired God of War 3 director Stig Asmussen to helm a team within Respawn out of a desire to diversify the studio’s output and prove he can do more than make shooters.

Zampella had only recently met with journalists and peers at The Game Awards, where Battlefield 6 was nominated for multiple awards. Battlefield 6 is the most successful game in series history, in part as a result of Zampella’s leadership. The legendary leader was given the reigns of the struggling multiplayer shooter franchise in 2021, with a goal of finding a viable future.

Zampella’s sudden death has shaken the industry, and many mourn his loss as the news started spreading.

“We are heartbroken by the loss of Vince Zampella, a creative leader whose work shaped generations of players and helped define what modern shooters and action games could be,” EA said in a statement.

“While his impact reached far beyond any one game or studio, we will remember Vince for how he showed up every day, trusting his teams, encouraging bold ideas, and believing in Battlefield and the people building it. We are deeply grateful for his leadership, his generosity, and the care he brought to everything he touched, and we will carry that forward with us.”

#4308. Killing Floor 3 Studio Announces Layoffs After Publishing Hire Spree

Lauren has experience in the gaming and esports space, writing news, guides, features, reviews, lists, conducting interviews, and more. Before joining the team at DualShockers, Lauren was a Features Writer at Adventure Gamers, a Guides Writer at Gameranx, as well as contributing as a News Writer at PCInvasion and Daily

Layoffs are always devastating for the video game industry and the people affected. Unfortunately, they have become all too common, and whether it’s a small studio or a large household name, it seems nobody is safe in today’s climate.

Tripwire Interactive, best known for the Killing Floor series, is the latest studio to be hit by layoffs. The studio was founded back in 2005, and Embracer Group acquired Tripwire Interactive through its former subsidiary, Saber Interactive, in 2022.

In our Killing Floor 3 Review, we go over what could have worked and what didn't in the end for Tripwire's latest game.

In a statement published on the official Tripwire Interactive X account, the studio says it “has undergone a workforce reduction, affecting 36 talented people across our studio. This was certainly not an easy decision, but unfortunately, a necessary one for the organization.”

Tripwire Interactive describes the impacted employees as “truly great people who are exceptional at their roles,” and vows to “help and support these individuals with compassion and dignity during transition.”

The team will continue to focus on Maneater 2, which was officially announced as part of Sony’s September State of Play. It’s expected to launch sometime in 2027.

As the name suggests, Maneater 2 is the sequel to 2021’s Maneater, an action-packed RPG where you are the biggest threat in the open-world oceans that you’ll traverse. There are new evolutions, discoveries to be made, and a whole lot of opportunities to become the villain.

It has also been confirmed that work will continue on Killing Floor 3, as the developers try to salvage the rocky start the game had when it was released back in July 2025. Killing Floor 3 reviews remain mixed among critics and players, and updates are still rolling out, containing new content and fixes.

This isn’t the first time this year that Tripwire Interactive has held layoffs. On March 4, the studio cut its workforce by 23 people, meaning this new round of layoffs brings Tripwire Interactive’s total this year to 59. Only time will tell if any of Tripwire Interactive’s projects will suffer from delays as a result of these layoffs.

Similar to this instance, a real reason wasn’t provided for the March 4 layoffs, instead citing: “As the gaming industry continues to evolve, so do the needs of our studios, which means understanding our long-term strategy and aligning with business realities where needed in order to stay focused on our key creative goals.”

Tripwire Interactive describes the impacted employees as “truly great people who are exceptional at their roles,” and vows to “help and support these individuals with compassion and dignity during transition.”

On November 4, 2026, Tripwire Presents, the publishing sector of Tripwire Interactive, announced that it would be expanding its business to include scaled publishing support for indie developers to help put the spotlight on indie titles from across a variety of genres. The purpose of the initiative is to provide greater visibility for self-published indie games that Tripwire believes fans will enjoy.

It has been confirmed that Tripwire Presents will continue to go ahead with their plans, and the games that have already been chosen are The Boss Gangster: Criminal Empire, Starforged Legacy, Mars Attracts, One-Eyed Likho, and Eslabong.

This round of redundancies adds another to the tally of alarmingly large video game industry layoffs just this year alone. Other examples include Sucker Punch making staff cuts shortly after the launch of the Complete Edition of Ghost of Yōtei, and, of course, the mass layoffs conducted by XBOX.

Another three rounds of XBOX layoffs are slated to begin this month and last into the new year.

#4307. Free-To-Play MOBA Pokémon Unite Is Shutting Down In March

The free-to-play MOBA Pokémon Unite will shut down in March, over five years after its 2021 launch. Although a gradual suspension of services begins today, fans will enjoy one last hurrah thanks to a big in-game event running for the remainder of the game’s lifecycle.

Launched in July 2021 for Switch before migrating to iOS and Android later that year, Pokémon Unite was billed as a friendlier take on the MOBA genre popularized by Dota 2 and League of Legends, thanks to its short matches (10 minutes) and simplified mechanics. Despite its initial popularity, the game is winding down and will go offline for good on March 23, 2027.

An End of Service notice on the game’s website reads,

“We offer our sincerest gratitude to the many Trainers who have played since service started for the Nintendo Switch version on July 21, 2021. We would like to express our thanks to everyone by holding a special event until service ends. The Pokémon Unite Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo competitive tournament (an event for Pokémon Unite only) will also be held as previously announced. We hope you continue to enjoy Pokémon Unite until the final day of service. After service ends, the 'Pokémon Unite Game Content Guidelines for Online Platforms' will no longer be published or maintained, and we will no longer provide support regarding use of Pokémon Unite videos and images.”

As of today, in-game sales of Aeos gems and Unite Club memberships/renewals have been suspended. Existing Unite Club members will continue to use their benefits until the end of the membership period.

On November 12, an update will kick off the aforementioned final special event, where players can obtain items such as all Unite licenses and Holoware that have appeared in the game up to that point. A library feature will also be added, letting players view certain records and in-game content even after the game shuts down on March 23. Those who don’t download the library feature before the shutdown date will not be able to get it afterward.

Qualifiers for the Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo Competitive tournament will take place as planned on December 5. After the game shuts down on March 23, players won't be able to log in to Pokémon Unite or play any battles. Only the library feature will remain accessible.

We enjoyed Pokémon Unite when it launched, with executive video editor Alex Van Aken scoring it an 8 out of 10 in his review, writing, “The game eats away the hours of my day as I reassuringly say to myself, 'Just one more match.' Battles play out with the spectacle that the Pokémon series is known for, and with so many abilities to choose from, no match feels the same as the last. The game’s simple mechanics and recognizable characters make for an approachable MOBA experience, and with a potential catalog of nearly 900 Pokémon to pick from, my hopes are high for the future of Pokémon Unite.”

#4300. Phantom Blade Zero Review – Wuxia Wonder Abounds

Rooted in Wuxian storytelling and scale, built on an impressively detailed combat system, and wrapped in a bloody Chinese martial underground that’s a genuine joy to play in, Phantom Blade Zero is a feat. It joins an echelon of action pedigree that includes Sekiro, Devil May Cry, Bayonetta, and just about any other action game you hold in high regard. It hails from developer S-Game, which has dabbled in mobile and smaller-scale games, and I’m shocked by what it’s pulled off with its triple-A action inauguration. But make no mistake: though Phantom Blade Zero is this team’s first crack at a game like this, it is an incredibly confident, strong debut.

Protagonist Soul is a stoic martial arts master betrayed by the Order he’s sworn his life to; he dies and returns to life with only 66 days to live. That’s enough time to settle his debts, repay his betrayers, and end a villainous conspiracy to seize full power of the Wulin realm. This narrative is Phantom Blade Zero's weakest link, but its premise adds enough mystery and tension to keep this Wuxian journey exciting through to its final, realm-shattering moments. Narrative bombshells drop not just through the game’s general fantasy-realism art direction, but also through anime scenes, opera puppet shows, animated brushstroke sequences, and more, highlighting Chinese culture and its integral place in Phantom Blade Zero.

The game features a staggering number of unique enemy types, and though the final hours get a bit repetitive, it’s admirable how long S-Game maintains such a high level of combat-oriented ecstasy. Soul’s access to weapons drives that exhilaration. Every weapon is wholly unique. Because the combat is combo-based, picking up a new weapon feels like unlocking a new character in a fighting game. Each has its own moveset and abilities, with later-game weapons featuring combo lists that look more at home in a Street Fighter menu. Add in the special, tide-turning weapons known as Phantom Edges, with limited charge-based uses, and there’s no shortage of permutations to delightfully experiment with.

Drawing on Chinese cinema, Phantom Blade Zero's setpiece bosses boast a sense of awe and scale only the genre's best typically offer. With virtually no repeat bosses, save for a few in separate trials, it’s impressive how many powerful figures I flayed, and how many delivered a unique fight. I also appreciate the checkpoints between boss phases, as they remove the frustrating repetition of replaying phase one again and again just to take another stab at the second phase I’m struggling with.

You’d be forgiven for assuming Phantom Blade Zero is a Soulslike, given its challenging bosses, interconnected world, and Phantom Bell checkpoints, this game’s equivalent of bonfires. It definitively isn’t, though. The challenge is much more surmountable; the game isn’t interested in making you die over and over, there are difficulty options, and you can equip accessories to make parries and dodges easier. World progression is materially different, too, as enemies don’t respawn after you kill them. It’s an interesting, perhaps blasphemous, choice for the genre, but it's surprisingly effective, adding a sense of worldbuilding and tangible progression I didn’t know I wanted from my action games. Soul is on a mission to remove evil, and mechanically, I’m doing just that. Enemies don’t respawn incoherently just because I heal and save.

Environmental features weave in and out of each other, and the architectural design and layout of these regions lead to many subsequent “aha” moments. S-Game infuses search-action elements into this exploration through the aforementioned Phantom Edges, some of which double as tools to unlock surprising new areas in both new and previously visited biomes. As a result, backtracking and exploration remain fresh. A lot of it is optional, as are some of Phantom Blade Zero's most rewarding elements, including its demanding “perfect” ending. Sadly, this renders other endings unsatisfying, with clear chunks intentionally missing.

Despite forays into the Uncanny Valley, Phantom Blade Zero is visually striking, and the action is brilliantly animated. It’s all set to genre-breaking music, too, with original metalcore songs, operatic choirs, 808s, and traditional Chinese instrumentation, creating a score as illustrious as the action it enhances.

Phantom Blade Zero is an astounding action achievement, almost unbelievably so for a game that is essentially a studio’s genre debut. It is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, one that recognizes the genre’s strengths and weaknesses and addresses both with fantastical Wuxian style. Though the action genre is always jam-packed with new releases, few are as special as Phantom Blade Zero.

Doesn’t look like it mattered much, however, as this has already been a big launch on iOS and Android — it probably helps that PC players aren't being entirely left out of the fun, since the game is already available there via XD's own cross-device platform TapTap.

XD Games announced today that Heartopia has reached the top spot on the App Store’s downloads page for free games, and it managed to do so in more than 50 countries and regions worldwide.

The developer is celebratig by offering players a lot of free stuff. If you're feeling lucky, you’ll find new outfits and furniture in three gacha banners (Gilded Acorn Exhibitions): Polar Hymn, The Frostguard, and Coolplayism.

XD Games says you can expect regular updates to add more content, through Fashionwaves and Festivals. In fact, the first season - Winter Frost - is already penciled in for sometime in late January, and it’s going to add appropriately wintery activities like ice skating and snowman-building.

In February, a My Little Pony collaboration event will kick off, bringing new inspired outfits, and vehicles to the game.

Heartopia is a clever mix of Animal Crossing, and The Sims. It’s a free-to-play life sim where you can create your own character, dress them up, build a home for them (and decorate it), and go about town visiting and playing with other players’ characters.

The game’s main feature is the ability to take on a hobby, and seven of those are available at launch. You can dig deep into each hobby, either alone or with others, and there’s a progression track dedicated to each one.

Whether you’re among the millions who downloaded the game already, or you intend to so soon, we’ve got a set of helpful guides to get you started. You should check out how to unlock and upgrade hobbies in Heartopia first, before you get deep into finding all cooking recipes. And, of course, this wouldn’t be a big game launch without a bunch of Heartopia codes for some free stuff.

#4295. Diablo 4's long-awaited Tower and its Leaderboards enter beta today, and there's no PTR funny business this time

Diablo 4's first big moment of 2026 is nearly upon us, and it's one feature many have been looking forward to for actual years.

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience launches today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside update 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

The beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the plan is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

The Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

The Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

The Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.

#4293. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

#4292. Nintendo Indie World Showcase Recap: Everything We Saw

The year is nearing its conclusion, and the last big AAA titles are rolling out one-by-one. But today, it was all about the independent titles on Nintendo's latest Indie World Showcase, highlighting new games from smaller indie teams coming to the Switch and Switch 2.

Here's everything we saw at the October 2026 Nintendo Indie World Showcase.

Today's Indie World Showcase started with a big headliner, as the long-awaited witch-life simulator Witchbrook got a release date. Chucklefish and Robtality's cozy magical world goes live on January 28, 2027.

Fans of 3D platformers should probably keep an eye on Winds of Viridia, which looks like a colorful game with a lot of interesting movement and exploration. Shark Jump's fantastical platformer is arriving next year, but if the wait's too long, a free demo is coming today on the eShop.

From one of the co-creators of Celeste, City of None has a gorgeous pixelated art style and colors that immediately remind me of Game Boy Color classics. It's a 2D platformer where you leap around, fight enemies, and explore the strange city around you. The jumping and fighting look solid, and I really like the mysterious atmosphere and art direction. City of None's set for sometime in 2027.

The sword-surfing adventure from the makers of Abzu and Journey is coming to Nintendo Switch 2 on October 29, 2026 - tomorrow! It's a gorgeous adventure that earned a Must-Play badge from us, so it's worth your time if you like the kinds of gorgeous, beautiful adventures Giant Squid (developer of Abzu) is known for.

Ah, raccoons. Nature's most adorable little scamps. If you and your friends have ever wanted to live out the dream of being a rambunctious band of raccoons wreaking havoc on the town, Dumpster Gang sets out to give you just that fantasy in March 2027.

I've already enjoyed quite a bit of Super Battle Golf on PC, so I'll tell you now: if you enjoy golf games and want some Mario Party annoy-your-friends antics wound around them, Super Battle Golf should be on your radar for its March 25, 2027 launch on Switch 2.

Another port of a PC multiplayer mainstay, the co-op physics-driven horror-looter R.E.P.O. is coming to Switch 2 in 2027. This is one for the crowd that likes to be scared one moment and laughing hysterically the next.

Rounding out the co-op section, Haunted Paws has you and a pal playing as a pair of pups searching for their person in a haunted mansion. The side-scrolling 3D look makes it seem like a less-scary Little Nightmares, and the concept is pretty fun. Look for this one on Switch and Switch 2 in May 2027, or try out the free demo later today.

Enjoy shrines, towns, and strange night-time journeys into the unknown? Follow a fox girl and her frog friend on an adventure through a strange island in Kitsune: The Journey of Adashino on Switch 2 and Switch in spring 2027. I've said it a few times in this recap, but wow, the art here is great.

The second entry in the slime-collecting, home-building sim adventure is coming to Switch 2. Pick up adorable slimes with your vacuum, build a home for them, and explore the Rainbow Island around you in January 2027. Plus, there's an exclusive in-game item for the Switch 2 version.

From the makers of Cozy Grove, this multiplayer game encourages players to build a home above the clouds with friends and explore the world around them. Spirit Crossing looks like a big world to make your own alongside your pals, starting November 16, 2026 on both Switch and Switch 2.

Want something a little sillier? My Arms Are Longer Now is a game about, well, really long arms. With numerous Australian comedians lending their vocal talents to the project, this seems like it could be a quirky, charming, and delightfully funny experience when it arrives on both Switch and Switch 2 on March 11, 2027.

#4290. Forgotten Memories: Definitive Edition is now free forever on iOS and Android

Free forever is a big promise, but Psychose Interactive has a fairly good reason for making it. Forgotten Memories: Definitive Edition, the studio’s survival horror from 2015, is now free on iOS and Android. No, this isn’t a weekend giveaway or one of Epic Games' weekly freebies. It’s staying that way.

You play as Rose Hawkins, who wakes up in an abandoned asylum while searching for a missing girl called Eden. It’s slow, third-person 90s-style horror, with puzzles, a torch and never quite enough ammo.

The asylum is split into different wings, and most of your time will be spent figuring out which locked door to open next. Our original review compared it closer to a point-and-click adventure, and with that many keys and locked doors, it’s probably true. The scares tend to land on the way back, once you’ve got what you came for and have to walk past the mannequins again.

It’s properly old-fashioned about the rest. You fight with a lead pipe and a bit of timing, and the torch battery runs down. Saving originally meant finding a computer and spending one of a limited stock of floppy disks, in the style of early Resident Evil, so dying could cost you half an hour.

Forgotten Memories: Remastered smooths some of the bugs out. It’s the rebuilt version that launched on mobile two years ago, with new lighting and checkpoint saves.

If the free one gets under your skin, the sale is the cheap way up. The Definitive Edition is free now on the App Store and Google Play. Forgotten Memories: Remastered is US$1.99 instead of US$6.99 on the App Store until Friday, November 13th.

Warhammer Survivors is a brutal spin-off of Vampire Survivors, pitting heroes from Warhammer 40,000 and Age of Sigmar against endless hordes of enemies while maintaining the addictive gameplay loop.

Few games have a title as accurate or descriptive to its core content as Warhammer Survivors. In a nutshell, itt’s Vampire Survivors gameplay, but with Warhammer 40,000 and Age of Sigmar characters, monsters, and levels, but with the difficulty turned up to eleven.

Well, that’s a bit of an unfair introduction. If Warhammer Survivors was just a cosmetic upgrade, they would have just released it as DLC in Vampire Survivors, rather than giving it its own dedicated game. After all, Vampire Survivors has invited Castlevania to its roster and added Contra too, so surely Space Marines wouldn’t look out of place?

Thankfully, Warhammer Survivors shakes up the gameplay and adds new tweaks to the familiar formula that makes it a worthwhile purchase for people who aren’t familiar with the tabletop game. Long-time Vampire Survivors fans just need to be aware that its Warhammer equivalent is a fair bit harder than the content they’ve beaten before.

At its core, Warhammer Survivors has the same gameplay loop as Vampire Survivors and its many clones. The player picks a hero, who then has to survive against endless hordes of enemies. The main gameplay gimmick is that the player cannot control how the character shoots: just how they move across the battlefield.

Throughout each level, the player earns experience points from killing enemies, and when they level up, they are given new weapons and upgrades that make it easier to destroy more foes. As time goes on, the enemies get stronger and grow in numbers, meaning careful movement becomes even more important.

There are also bosses that appear throughout the stage, which are outlined in a neon green aura. Slaying these bosses results in crates being dropped with level upgrades. These are important, as if a weapon is sufficiently levelled, then a crate could carry its improved version, such as the Boltgun transforming into the Heavy Boltgun, which has a drastically improved fire rate.

Dying on a run isn’t the end of the world, as the player can find coins strewn throughout each stage that can be spent on static buffs and upgrades. These make future runs easier, so the player has a greater chance of surviving later stages.

Warhammer Survivors keeps this gameplay loop intact, though it splits everything across two worlds. On the main menu, the player selects the “Universe”: Warhammer 40,000 and Age of Sigmar, the latter of which is the modern replacement for Warhammer Fantasy (RIP). They have their own stages, characters, and enemies, with no direct crossovers between the two.

Technically, there is content that connects the two, as the upgrades unlocked are shared between the two, meaning working hard in one helps out the other. There are also non-franchise-specific levels that they share, like the Hobby Table, but for the most part, the Warhammer 40,000 and Age of Sigmar parts of the game are separate.

A new indie inspired by Vampire Survivors tasks players with defending their home computer from an onslaught of 2000s-era viruses.

So, if Warhammer Survivors is just Vampire Survivors with Ork Boyz, then is it worth buying? Well, there are some key differences that justify it existing as its own game, rather than DLC for Vampire Survivors.

In Vampire Survivors, all the weapons are tied to the player character. Warhammer Survivors changes this with its Follower system, as characters are now unlocked alongside their weapon when the player levels up. This means they follow the selected hero around, and their attacks will originate from them.

The Follower system might not seem like a big addition, but needing to account for the changing starting position of attacks makes the gameplay considerably more challenging. This is especially true for the Garlic-type weapon users, which have a static area-of-effect centred on their hero. In Warhammer Survivors, the party members move around after the player, meaning the player has to guide them, like a kite, into the enemy hordes.

The other big difference in Warhammer Survivors is how it handles end of stage bosses. In Vampire Survivors, if the player spends too long in a stage, they’ll eventually be attacked by the Grim Reaper and quickly killed. Warhammer Survivors replaces the manifestation of death with the Extremis Bosses: foes that appear at the twenty-five minute mark for an epic fight.

The Follower system might not seem like a big addition, but needing to account for the changing starting position of attacks makes the gameplay considerably more challenging.

The Extremis Bosses can’t be faced without preparation, however, as the player needs to unlock a specific item in each stage to be able to damage them. If the player doesn’t have this item, then the boss will be invincible, and it will automatically kill the hero in a cutscene.

The enemies the player faces on each stage can also have unique gimmicks, usually tied to their bosses. It’s possible for Tyranids to buff their weaker units, making them considerably faster, while the followers of Nurgle can summon massive poison-spewing chimneys, creating damaging areas for the player to walk through.

The Orks of Warhammer 40,000 easily have the best gimmick, as they can call a mighty “Waaagh”, bringing endless waves of units against the player until it ends. Surviving a Waaagh can be one of the trickiest parts of the Ork stage, unless the player prepares lots of AoE attacks to survive the horde.

The studio behind Vampire Crawlers has revealed how the game came about, thanks to its relationship with the creator of Vampire Survivors.

The new additions to Warhammer Survivors make the game considerably harder than the source game. And make no mistake: I adore Vampire Survivors and have purchased it on multiple platforms. I have endured countless runs with my boy Poe, facing the creatures of the night with nothing but a piece of Garlic and a dream, and came out the other side.

Warhammer Survivors ramps the difficulty up in a few ways. The Follower system means the origin point of your weapons keeps moving around, making it harder to accurately fire at enemies. This isn’t as much of a problem with targeted weapon users, like grenades, but AoE and shooter characters are harder to predict, as they keep moving while shooting.

The changes to bosses are also a point against the game, because Warhammer Survivors does an extremely poor job of conveying exactly what items are needed to be “Prepared” for facing the Extremis Bosses. The best clues the player gets is seeing what items are always available in each stage, as well as blanked out menus that fill out if they happen to use the correct upgrades.

There’s far too little information about what items are needed to face the Extremeis Bosses, especially as the blanked out menu only appears after a twenty-five minute run, which is hard to reach on a good day. Most players aren’t going to bother doing trial and error: they’ll just Google the answers as soon as the game launches, so why bother obfuscating it?

It also bears mentioning that the Age of Sigmar characters are way less useful than their 40,000 equivalents. The Warhammer 40,000 roster includes gun and grenade users, while the ranged Age of Sigmar characters tend to be much slower. Thankfully, the upgrades menu stays the same between rosters, so it’s possible to grind with the Warhammer 40,000 cast for stat upgrades, in order to help out their fantasy equivalents.

There are also times when the game will just kill the player with no recourse. The Age of SIgmar stages are particularly bad for this, with enemy cavalry units randomly appearing and rushing across the stage, pushing the player into a wall and instantly killing them in a way that’s impossible to avoid.

The sub bosses fought in each stage also have far, far too much health. I’ve sat there for what felt like an eternity with maxed out weapons, stunlocking a boss into place, while damage numbers just rack up, and they won’t die. It’d be fine if their gameplay made them challenging foes to match their mighty health bar, but many of them are just regular enemies with bigger sprites.

The changes to Warhammer Survivors do provide an extra layer of challenge for those coming from the source material, and I’d be lying if I said I didn’t enjoy the new additions and wrinkles: it just needs a few more tweaks and balance checks for the game to be as good as it can be.

This review covers Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 and why players should play it.

The Warhammer franchise has a reputation for being extremely dark in tone, especially 40,000. The Imperium of Man isn’t exactly a lovely place to exist, between the constant threat of Xeno invasion, the corrupting influence of Chaos present in the souls of mankind, and the rampant corruption within society itself.

Warhammer Survivors is a rare example of Warhammer being tongue-in-cheek and referential. This can be seen through its many nods to the actual game and its history, especially the weapons, such as exploding d6s hitting the board, Nuln Oil slowing foes down, the measuring tape increasing damage AoE, and the experience point booster being called White Dwarf.

The highlight of this approach is the Hobby Table stage, where the player fights off monsters on a crafting table, the kind used by many real-life fans of the tabletop game. The developers had mentioned in the past that the Hobby Table stage is a nod to Micro Machines, and it shows, being easily the most fun level in Warhammer Survivors.

The visuals and overall aesthetic of Warhammer Survivors are close to that of Vampire Survivors, and like the Boltgun series, the approach is mired in retro goodness. Few Warhammer games have managed to cram as many foes onto the screen as this one, making Warhammer Survivors one of the few titles to ever capture the essence of the beloved artwork from the series, save shown through a 16-bit filter.

Warhammer Survivors doesn’t try to tell a story: it’s about throwing iconic heroes from the franchise against familiar foes. It’s clear the people who made the game are huge fans of the source material, and that love shines throughout the experience.

The new layer of difficulty in Warhammer Survivors can be frustrating at times, but it also feels necessary for helping distinguish it from Vampire Survivors. If the player can soldier through the hard moments, then they’ll get another massive dose of Survivors gameplay and content, which is likely a huge selling point on its own for people who are still addicted to the original.

Warahmmer Survivors justifies itself as a separate entity throughout plenty of new characters and stages, with enough gameplay gimmicks to ensure it’s not just a reskin. The difficulty can be frustrating at times, but people don’t sign up for a Survivors-like to have an easy time. Warhammer Survivors will satisfy people looking for more of the familiar but different enough to not be a rehash, while still paying tribute to the universes that won over fans worldwide.

#4286. Rocket Rally brings 30-second arcade rally races to iOS and Android

You've got half a minute and one thumb to win

When we reviewed Major Mayhem, the iPhone 4S was brand new. Rocket Jump, the studio behind it, is back, this time with Rocket Rally, which is a physics-driven arcade rally racer that’s up for pre-registration on iOS and Android.

If it predates your phone, Major Mayhem was a one-finger cover shooter. Your soldier ran between cover by himself, and you held a finger down to fire. It was brash and silly and very easy to pick up for a minute, and it also earned a Silver Award from us.

Rocket Rally takes that one-input approach to rally. Races last thirty seconds, you play it one-handed in portrait, and the cars run on a custom arcade physics system the studio built itself. Time Attack and Head to Head sit alongside Rally X4 and Rally X6.

Around that is a solo career set in locations around the world, where you buy cars, upgrade them and build up a garage, plus daily online competition. There are over 100 stages across four environments at launch, with more promised every month, and hundreds of cosmetic options for your liveries.

Thirty seconds doesn’t feel like a lot, but I think it’s the right length for something like this. I don’t see myself completing a three-lap race on my phone while I’m en route somewhere, but a rally stage before my bus reaches its stop? I can see myself getting behind that. Of course, that means it leaves no time to learn handling that doesn’t make sense straight away.

Rocket Rally is expected to release on December 15th, although that could change. It will be free-to-play with ads. Pre-registration is currently open on the App Store and Google Play.

If you're into proper racing, most races on our list of the best racing games for iOS take a good deal longer than thirty seconds.

Battlefield 6 has pushed back its next season by nearly a month in order to refine Season 2 content and implement more of players' feedback.

Battlefield Studios has released its first official communication in 2026. Rather than unveil the second season of Battlefield 6, however, the developer instead announced a delay. The currently ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off. Given the current sentiment around the game, this news isn’t surprising in the least.

In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios said that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.

The developer did not offer any hints about Season 2, but there’s an incredibly brief teaser trailer featuring a soldier wearing a gas mask emerging from an environment drenched in toxic gas.

Given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1. Of course, this may just be a visual piece that doesn’t reflect the gameplay of Season 2.

Escalating the fight with new threats on the battlefield.Season 2 begins February 17. pic.twitter.com/fGMegJJuTj

What we are getting news of today, however, is the game’s next patch. This extension update is going to arrive next week, on January 20, when Season 1 was supposed to end. It’s bringing new weekly challenges to the game, but its biggest addition is yet another Bonus Path to the battle pass. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

Similar to other Bonus Paths, the new Frostfire Bonus Path can be completed alongside the Season 1 battle pass. You’ll need 110 Bonus Path Points in total if you want to earn everything it has to offer, with each tier requiring 10 points. It is worth noting, however, that Frostfire Points are only earned through weekly challenges, meaning there won’t be any bonus challenges associated with it.

Frostfire includes several new customisation rewards, of course, such as a Weapon Package, soldier skin, XP boosts and the usual run of unlocks.

Though the latest blog post may be devoid of any real details on Season 2, BF Studios confirmed that Battlefield Labs will play a larger role in offering a preview of what’s to come, so it’s entirely possible that the testing initiative will soon open its doors to players with an early look at some of the maps and other content planned for Season 2.

#4283. Murals Interview: How To Create A Mascot Who's Not As Annoying As Ocarina Of Time's Navi

Scott Baird is a Contributor from the UK with over a decade of video game writing experience.

Murals is an upcoming action RPG by Dlala Studios that, on the surface, looks a great deal like Hades. The concept of Murals involves twisted and humorous takes on classic fairy tales, like Rapunzel, which is an idea that’s more commonplace than the straight tellings of those stories, with everyone from Disney to Alan Moore turning fables on their head.

Originality isn’t the golden ticket to a video game being enjoyable, and in this case, the differences from genre norms are in the gameplay, not the story. While Murals might look like countless isometric action RPG roguelikes on Steam, it’s going for a linear, narrative-based progression, with crafted levels and enemies, rather than relying on randomness.

Playing it straight is a surprisingly bold move, and it runs counter to the story of Murals. DualShockers recently visited Dlala’s offices to preview Murals, where we got the chance to speak to the studio’s CEO, AJ Grand-Scrutton, about the many choices that went into making Murals.

Q: The idea of fables and fairy tales being twisted and viewed through a modern lens has been done many times before. Were there any specific examples that inspired Murals?

Grand-Scrutton: So obviously the source material was where we went to initially, the grim stuff and the Hans Christian Andersen. But I mean, I loved American McGee's Alice. I was a massive fan of that. There's a lot of like comic books as well, like Fables. I love Wolf Among Us. So I love that familiarity that you recognize the story, but enough difference that you don't feel you're just retreading old ground.

Q: Have any video games inspired the gameplay or design of Murals?

Grand-Scrutton: Obviously, Murals is isometric and it's got pretty chaotic moment to moment. So a lot of modern Roguelikes, your Hades, et cetera. I struggle with permadeath, especially as I've got older. I'm quite impatient and moody. And so kind of what I really loved was like the moment to moment in a lot of modern roguelikes, but I didn't necessarily get on very well with the permadeath loop. So that was a big influence for how Murals came about.

Like, can we take some of those chaotic moment to moment experiences; those combat augmentation systems and deliver them in like a bit longer form content? And also like, you know, weird influences in there as well. You know, like a lot of our world building Psychonauts and a lot of double fine stuff was really prominent in our minds. And, you know, classic combat games like DMC, Bayonetta.

But yeah, it was really just about us trying to capture an experience we didn't feel we could fully play out there already.

We traveled to China to chat with Soulframe about his upcoming action RPG, Phantom Blade Zero.

Q: The protagonist is mostly silent in Murals, with most of the talking being done by the character’s sidekick, Loaf. How do you go about designing a talkative side character like Loaf in a way that makes them likeable. Were there any concerns they’d become another Navi from Ocarina of Time?

Grand-Scrutton: Yeah, so, I mean, we always are very aware that our style of writing can become... Every character can feel like that very quickly for people. I mean, I think if you look at Battletoads, you look at Illusion Island and you look at Murals, you can tell it's very much like the same writing team that have done them.

Loaf is kind of, in a weird way, is obviously this sentient sketch come to life. He's the most naturally written character because it's often me and Kelsy, my lead writer, just typing what we're thinking about situations or stupid commets. Like, often we'll just be on calls and we'll play through the game. And Kelsy, as well as writing, she actually is Loaf. She does the voice of Loaf. And we'll almost do our own little director's commentaries as we're playing the game to figure out where Loaf comments should go and what would Loaf say in this situation.

I think with humour, comedy in games, we're not unique. There's other people that do comedy games, but it's still quite a niche. And I think you kind of just have to lean into what you are. And I think that we are that self-referential type of humour. We do the fourth wall breaking. There is the modern label of the meta-level stuff in there. And I think it'd be easy for us to go half-arsed or half-cocked on it. But we just kind of leant into it. This is what we find funny, and that's kind of how we write the game.

Q: Why go for such a basic, sketch outline design for Loaf?

Grand-Scrutton: Yeah, I love the juxtaposition. So obviously, as you've seen from the couple of murals you've played, the characters that live in the world are hand-animated, but they've still got depth to them.

The invasive forces, which is the distorted, the enemies, and the hero, the player, are fully animated. And I love this idea that Loaf was just... the hero just made this rough sketch in their notebook or something and accidentally got brought to life. I love Doodlebob, who is definitely an influence from the SpongeBob cartoons.

I just think there's something really nice about... we've got these animated characters that are still not realistic, but almost like they make sense. And then Loaf is just a cartoon. He doesn't really have the rules of physicality that a humanoid would have. He is just who he is. And I think that just gave us some really fun opportunities, and it let us do some silly things with him.

An interview with Jonathan Blow about the making and future of Order of the Sinking Star.

Q: Is Murals intended as a linear experience, or is there more of a roguelike/Hades-style progression, with a hub area, random layouts, and upgrades sticking between runs.

Grand-Scrutton: No, it's very, very linear. Like, we're always up front about that because we know how misleading it can be when you see like an isometric action game. It's very linear. Like, the only real elements of random to it are the order you get the Eeries in.

So, you know, if you do a playthrough, you may get different Eeries to someone else doing the exact same playthrough. But the story, the quests, the enemies themselves, that is all very sculpted.

Q: In the Murals preview, there’s a very generous window for being able to dash out of attacks. Is this planned to be maintained for the final build or is the gameplay balance being tweaked still, out of fear it could make the combat too easy?

Grand-Scrutton: Yes, no, maybe to all the above. We're still tweaking. We'll be tweaking until my Tech Director pries it from my cold dead hands. We definitely have gone generous with a lot of things like this. I think the difficulty you're playing in general is probably on the easier side of what we would balance the final game.

You know, we're looking to make it customizable though, right? In terms of like enemy health, enemy damage, amount of health, you probably notice in the build you're playing right now that you always have enough health drops to get full health basically. That would probably be the generous setting on the slider for health drops. But I think the dash serves a very specific purpose in our game, obviously it's not unique at all.

But we've got a lot of boss fights, environmental hazards and other enemies as you progress through the game where giving the players a generous dash meant we could get more chaotic with the experience. I think, you know, if you look at our game and compare to some of our other peers, I think that's one of the slight difference of our moment to moment.

I think we're not a one versus one experience. We're not one versus many. We're like a one versus some is what I like to say. But we do reasonably small spaces with a reasonably large amount of enemies. And so while the play space is quite chaotic, we wanted to give the player simple enough verbs that they could control so they never felt like the game was being unfair.

DualShockers spoke with the developers of Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember about why a sequel was made and how the gameplay has changed from its predecessor.

Q: Some of the enemies have a flashing light before they attacked. Is this hinting at a parry mechanic for the full version of the game? Do you dare release a game in 2027 with no parrying?

Grand-Scrutton: I mean, we are daring to not release. No, there's no parry. They're very generous tells on some of the enemies that do more damage. We definitely discussed parrying really early on. We discussed parrying, we discussed blocking. But it just, it felt a bit like a hat on a hat for what we were making. Like, you know, we like, we believe in like, depth through simplicity. This is not a big combo based game.

You know, it's not even as combo laden as like our Battletoads was. It's a very simple amount of inputs with like varying weapons and a lot of depth comes through the power-ups. And the problem I find with parrying is like, modern games are amazing.

Like, you know, Expedition 33, all these games are absolutely outstanding. I find when I play them that my gameplay just becomes around parrying. All I do is parry. Like, in a lot of ways, although I love them, I play them multiple times.

I felt that learning to do the block timing in the Arkham games made the combat a little bit less exciting for me because I actually certainly changed my entire strategy in those games to be let the enemy come to me. And I just didn't want that for this. I didn't want the focus to be on parry timing. I wanted the focus to just be like, have a little bit of fun controlled chaos.

Q: Finally, why choose Murals as the game’s name?

Grand-Scrutton: Yeah, we are traditionally, not necessarily publicly, very awful at doing project codenames. Like, the codename for Battletoads was Frogspawn, which is not the most... And the codename for Illusion Island was Illusions because we weren't originally going to call it that.

So Project Murals was the codename for Murals because we love the idea that these worlds are like these fairy tales brought to life by through these painted murals the creator has done. But the team will tell you, I have this obsession, I think Pokémon is the greatest name for a franchise ever because I love a name that is memorable and it's also the name of a thing in the game or in the world. And I love the idea of us having murals because the levels are called murals and it's also the name and it makes sense.

So it's kind of like this dragon I've been chasing and it just fit the game and it worked for me. And there's some funniness in there as well to me through some previous titles we've worked on and stuff in the past where we've tried to put forward names for things and we've been told that the majority of the...

We had a game we were working on years ago, years and years ago, and it was around animatronics. And this was years back. I mean, it was before it was necessarily common lingo but I really wanted to call it Tronics and I was like, oh, how cool is this name? And we got told by our partners at the time that no one knows what an animatronic is so we couldn't do it. And then Five Nights at Freddy's came out a year later and I was like, everyone knows what animatronic is, look.

And we've had similar things with this, like when we'd kind of pitched this to people before the name Murals, people were like, I don't think anyone's gonna really know what a mural is. And I was like, I'm pretty sure people know what a mural is. So it was nice to kind of have that control ourselves.

The development team behind Disgaea Mayhem discusses balancing an action RPG while maintaining insane level and damage numbers.

#4281. Full FC 26 Team of the Year promo brings free Hero upgrades and another unstoppable Claudia Pina

The FC 26 Team of the Year brings new end-game special cards for meta favourites and Icons, as well as upgrades for free Heroes.

EA Sports has revealed the much-anticipated Ultimate Team of the Year cards for the 2025/26 season, including a slew of meta favourites from the likes of the evergreen Virgil van Dijk, super-fast Kylian Mbappe and unplayable queen of FC 26 Claudia Pina.

Elsewhere Lionesses Alessia Russo, Lucy Bronze and Leah Williamson feature alongside now-obligatory Barcelona duo Alexia Putellas and Aitana Bonmati. On the men’s side, Arsenal’s title tilt sees Declan Rice and William Saliba make the first 11, while Champions League holders PSG have the most players from a single team, with Ousmane Dembele, Vitinha and Nuno Mendes adding both rapid speed and technical prowess to proceedings.

However, the Team of the Year selection hasn’t been without controversy. The FC 26 TOTY promo is voted for by players, you probably cast your vote by selecting time-limited gold cards yourself, but that method has led some to question whether the Team of the Year is more of a popularity contest than a true measure of performance. #4279. Murals Preview: Frantic Fairy Tale Fun

Murals is taking old fairy tales and filtering them through an action RPG lens, while injecting the stories with a fresh dose of British humor.

Fairy tales have been deconstructed and shown through a modern lens so many times that subversions are almost as common as straight tellings of the original stories. Murals is an upcoming action RPG that takes a comedic, subversive look at classic kids' stories, wrapped in an addictive gameplay loop familiar to fans of the big hits of the past few years.

Roguelike action RPGs have exploded in popularity, especially on PC, with gamers becoming hooked on brutally difficult gameplay merged with random elements that offer near-infinite replayability. On the surface, Murals seems cut from the same cloth as something like Hades, being an action RPG with an isometric viewpoint, where a long hero dashes around, avoiding attacks, while unleashing an increasingly larger arsenal at their foes.

DualShockers visited developer Dlala Studios at their home base for a hands-on preview of Murals. This consisted of playing the first two chapters and experiencing an in-development build of the game that is still being tweaked and worked on. What’s here is impressive, especially in terms of the aesthetics, with gorgeous visuals on display for Murals’ fairy-tale world.

The Murals preview I played featured two stages: Little Briar Rose (the story that formed the basis for Sleeping Beauty), and Rapunzel. The story starts with the protagonist, whose appearance can best be described as “Player 2 April O’Neil,” waking up in a mysterious new world with no memory of how they got there.

The protagonist of Murals doesn't talk much, but when they do, they have branching dialogue options. Sadly, the game immediately says that these have no bearing on the gameplay and are just for flavor, so the choices may as well not exist. While I'm not expecting some Mass Effect-style consequences for every dialogue choice, it'd be nice if some of the responses had some kind of bearing on the gameplay.

The protagonist doesn't talk much because they're soon joined by Loaf, the game's mascot character. Loaf is a poorly drawn doodle that resembles an eraser with lizard-like plates on its back. Loaf quickly sets the comedic tone of the story, with Monty Python-esque retorts to the silliness of their situation, before the two are joined by Slash Gordon, the player’s trusty blade.

The chapters of Murals I experienced involved solving the locals' problems, such as helping an insomniac Sleeping Beauty or freeing a trapped Rapunzel by climbing her hair up the tower. There was also an overarching story involving a mysterious being known as The Creator, who looks like a smug art critic and seems to pull the strings from afar, guiding the protagonist along.

Twisted Tower is a terrifyingly twisted fairy tale that's done its homework.

One reliable ally the player has between battles is Magic Dave, voiced by legendary UK comedian Bob Mortimer. He’s the Resident Evil 4 Merchant of the game, providing upgrades (called Eeries) between stages, while exchanging witty banter with Toast.

The comedy in Murals is going to be love it or hate it. Saying it’s steeped in British irreverence is an understatement, and that sentence alone might be off-putting to some. A great comparison is the works of the late great Terry Pratchett: that provides a metric of Britishness the player should expect.

Dlala Studios is no stranger to pretty 2D games, having previously created the modern Battletoads game, as well as Disney Illusion Island. Murals marks the studio's departure from established intellectual properties and into publishing, which is why fairy tales were the company's next stop, since they're in the public domain.

Easily the high point of Murals is its visuals. Each level in Murals is a stunning, hand-drawn piece of artwork, where every room appears lovingly crafted and filled with little touches to admire while exploring.

Each level in Murals is a stunning, hand-drawn piece of artwork, with every room lovingly crafted and filled with little touches to admire while exploring. The same is true of the character artwork, with everything polished to perfection. The level of detail is especially impressive, considering Murals is still being developed, yet the team already has the aesthetic nailed down.

What once started out as a subgenre of NES classics has now become a typically hand-drawn set of video games that never fail to impress.

The only exception to the pretty visuals is the enemies in Murals, which are 3D models and nowhere near as visually impressive as the stages or NPCs. The monsters are quite generic and don't feel like they match the fairy-tale world they exist in, with designs that could fit into pretty much any action RPG.

The boss monsters are similarly whelming, with the giant frog faced in the Little Briar Rose stage doing the same jumping attack over and over again, only adding mobs to his move pool. In contrast, the final encounter of the Rapunzel stage is just waves of enemies, with no big boss in sight.

Fairy tales are full of creative villains who could be repurposed for use in video games. Just look at The Wolf Among Us for only one example among many. The enemies in Murals need an injection of creativity in both their design and battle strategy if the game wants to keep the player's interest.

It's impossible to play Murals and not compare it to Hades or its sequel. Just looking at a gameplay video on the Steam page, the comparisons are easy to see. It’s impossible to deny that Murals has Hades DNA, with the same basic combat loop, even though it takes a drastically different approach.

In Murals, the player has a choice of melee weapons (the sword named Slash Gordon and the hammer called the Wolfhammer in the demo), a ranged weapon with recharging ammo, and a super move that builds up over the battle, all of which are used to destroy foes. The player can dash to avoid enemy attacks and must survive waves of enemies through chains of rooms, with liberal health drops between areas.

As someone who was brutalized by Hades 2 in the past, one mechanic in Murals' combat immediately stuck out. When swinging a weapon or using a ranged attack, it's possible to perform a dash and gain invincibility frames. This makes the combat significantly easier than in similar games, as the player doesn't have to commit to attacks in the same way as they would in, say, a FromSoftware game, leaving them locked into a position where they can be countered.

Sébastien Benard's action roguelike has resurfaced with a release window after several years of radio silence.

The quick dash is more effective when using Slash Gordon, as it synergizes well with a swift weapon. This isn't to say that the Wolfhammer isn't also broken in its own way, as it has a breath weapon-style attack that can be merged with a Frost Rune to perform multiple hits that each have a chance of inflicting the Freeze status effect on an enemy, drastically increasing the chance of paralyzing them.

This makes the combat significantly easier than in similar games, as the player doesn't have to commit to attacks in the same way as they would in, say, a FromSoftware game, leaving them locked into a position where they can be countered.

Murals is still a work-in-progress, so there’s plenty of time for developers to tweak the gameplay balance. What’s here is considerably easier than many of the action RPGs on the market, but the reason for that could be related to the fact that it’s a mostly linear, story-based game, with few roguelike elements.

The levels in Murals might look like the randomly connected rooms of countless roguelikes, but the stages have been crafted and designed to tell a story, including NPC encounters, puzzles, and even side quests. While there are some random elements, such as how the upgrades/Eeries are handled, the bulk of the game is a planned affair, which explains why it’s easier than its contemporaries.

Each level in Murals is a stunning, hand-drawn piece of artwork, where every room appears lovingly crafted and filled with little touches to admire while exploring

It's a bold move to go for a linear approach in a market so consumed with randomness, especially when Murals uses a gameplay style and overall aesthetic that’s tied to roguelikes. That being said, there’s plenty of room for a more focused and narrative-driven title that uses the gameplay loop of familiar titles, especially when the levels look this good.

Murals has a ton of potential and an amazing pedigree behind it. Dlala Studios has produced some amazing titles in the past, and the fact that the game is so polished and impressive at this point in development is a feat unto itself. The hard part is going to be tweaking the combat to make it satisfying for everyone, meaning some strict difficulty modifiers could be the answer.

The comedic writing and tone in Murals are trickier, as they're so baked into the game’s identity, yet also have the potential to miss the mark. It’s the kind of thing that someone will know they’re going to enjoy within a short period of time, and hopefully, Mural’s subversive take on fairy tales is as appealing to the audience as its combat.

#4277. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4273. Here's The Best Graphics And Performance Mode For Phantom Blade Zero On PlayStation 5

Phantom Blade Zero is out now for everyone as a console exclusive on PlayStation 5 and on PC via Steam and the Epic Games Store as well. If you missed it, it's my favorite action game of the year so far, and you can read why in Game Informer's Phantom Blade Zero review. That explains why I think you should check the game out; Game Informer's list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks will get you some key information I wish I had when I started the game; and this guide I wrote up about the requirements you need to get the best ending in Phantom Blade Zero will help you find all story-critical content in the game.

However, you're looking for advice on which of the three visual modes Phantom Blade Zero offers you should use on your PS5. This here piece is for you.

Phantom Blade Zero has three visual modes on PS5 Pro: Quality, Balanced, and Performance. I tested all three. My personal favorite was Balanced, which gives you an upscaled (checkerboarded) 4K resolution at 40 FPS, as long as you have a 120Hz TV with VRR. If you have a 120Hz TV, it likely has VRR because most major manufacturers include it with 120Hz. I like this mode because the upscaled 4K looks beautiful, just a hair less than native 4K, and if you aren't someone super trained on those details, I'd wager you won't notice the difference. The best part is that this mode offers 40 FPS gameplay, which, contrary to how math works, is halfway between 30 FPS and 60 FPS; I'm not kidding, look it up. As such, 40 FPS feels much smoother than 30 FPS, and you're still getting crisp 4K resolution. It's a win-win for me and my go-to mode when a game offers it. That said, if you don’t have a PS5 Pro, you won’t see this Balanced mode.

The Performance mode offers an upscaled 2K resolution with a pretty locked 60 FPS. Phantom Blade Zero is an extremely fast, fluid action game, so I think many people will want the buttery smoothness of 60 FPS gameplay. If that's you, pick the Performance mode. Sure, its resolution is lower, and it will look blurrier and less crisp than the other two modes, but if you aren't switching back and forth often or looking at side-by-side images, you likely won't notice.

Quality mode is native 4K resolution (absolutely beautiful, the best visual image you can get playing Phantom Blade Zero), but at 30 FPS... and for a game like this, I don't think 30 FPS does it justice. I don't really recommend this mode for combat, but if you're just waltzing around Wulin, grabbing screenshots and such, turn it on and bask in the wonders of developer S-Game's art team. Note: There is an option for ray tracing on PS5 Pro. I tested all three graphics modes with it on and off and noticed zero performance changes or issues. So, use ray tracing – it’s nice!
