#4272. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

It's only been a couple of months that we've known about the existence of Diablo 5, and as such there are a ton of open questions about the direction it'll take. Blizzard teased a few fundamentals during BlizzCon 2026, like the fact that it'll take place in a Sanctuary that's been completely overtaken by Diablo and his minions, and that there will no longer be any traditional towns or safe havens to hide from the bad guys. It's been clear to me that Blizzard is doubling down on the horror-driven bleakness that defined the first game in the series, and there are blatant call-backs to the series' roots in the itemization and procedurally generated environments, but there's still a lot left unanswered about what it'll be like to actually play Diablo 5.

Chris Wilson, co-creator of Path of Exile and noted Diablo 2 mega fan, has been encouraged by everything Blizzard has shown of Diablo 5, but has one concern based on the messaging so far. Referencing comments from Diablo leadership at this year's BlizzCon suggesting Blizzard is surveying all generations of players from Diablo 1 to 4, Wilson says he's worried Blizzard might be trying to appeal to too many different audiences at once. He points out that Blizzard didn't even label Diablo an action-RPG series until Diablo 2: Lord of Destruction, and that Diablo 3 and 4 each appeal to a different type of player as well.

"This means that when you survey Diablo players and say 'what would you like in a Diablo 5, how can we get you to play it?', you're gonna get many different answers, and I worry that some of these answers might be slightly mutually exclusive," Wilson says in an interview with Destin Legarie. "I'm optimistic by what they showed because there's heavy Diablo 2 signaling, and that's really cool. I just would urge caution, of, it's OK to not appeal to every Diablo player as long as the product that's made is really fun for the core audience you're targeting, and I'm sure they are thinking of the core audience. Like, I'm simplifying it a lot here, but that's my one worry, really, that they go a bit too broad.

"There's a saying, if you make a game for everyone, you make a game for no one," Wilson concludes.

I understand where Wilson's coming from as a fellow Diablo 1+2 diehard, but it seems a little premature to be worrying about a too-safe Diablo 5 based on such limited information. There are all sorts of reasons a developer might survey fans of a series from different entry points, and regardless of Blizzard's reasoning, everything we've seen so far points to the darkest Diablo yet, which if anything stands in stark contrast to a game like Diablo 3. Meanwhile, the aforementioned return to procedural generation and Diablo 2-style itemization further suggests an embrace of the series' roots rather than some broad-strokes appeal to every generation of Diablo player.

This could very well be pure hopium, but the overall vibe I'm getting as a lifelong Diablo player, and as someone who attended this year's BlizzCon and spoken directly with Blizzard, is that the original Diablo is at the forefront of the studio's mind as it works on Diablo 5. To be very, very clear, that's just the collective impression that's formed in my head over dozens of interviews, panels, and videos scanned, and not something I was explicitly told by Blizzard, but it's exactly what I'm hoping for nonetheless.

Diablo 4's nostalgic new season has convinced me that we need a Diablo 1 remake more than Diablo 5

#4268. Heartopia surprise launches on Steam and shockingly, everyone seems to be happy

Heartopia players didn't actually end up having to wait too long to play the game on Steam, which is certainly not what anyone expected.

Heartopia has officially arrived on Steam, only a little over a week after it launched on iOS and Android. When the game’s release date was announced back in December, developer XD said it was pushing back the Steam release without offering any hints about how long the delay was going to be.

While the game can be played on PC through TapTap, the developer’s own emulator, many had been anticipating the Steam launch. So you can imagine that when the free-to-play life sim game surprisingly showed up on Valve’s platform on Saturday, there were a lot of happy people.

Heartopia’s Steam release has, much like mobile launch, been a success. We do know that the game reached the number one spot across app stores in over 50 countries, and though the Steam numbers may not be as record-breaking, everything is looking pretty good.

The game peaked at a decent 28,815 concurrent players (via SteamDB) on Steam one day after it launched, and considering how sticky it has been with the majority of those players so far - and the fact the launch itself was a surprise - there’s every chance those figures will improve over the course of this week as it picks up momentum.

Steam user reviews have similarly been quite positive, with the overall rating currently sitting at Mostly Positive, based on over 1,400 reviews.

You’re still need either a Google, Facebook, or Apple account to log into the game, same as you would on mobile. The Steam version does support cross-play with other platforms, so you’ll be able to play with your friends on mobile.

We’ve been playing a lot of Heartopia ourselves, and have been updating and expanding our guides. If you’re looking to get started, such as with how to add and play with friends, how to regain Energy, and how to unlock home plots, our guides offer the best place to start.

While the 2025 reveal of the Switch 2 came with many surprises, none were as unexpected as The Duskbloods. It's a Switch 2 exclusive, multiplayer-only title from FromSoftware, the developer behind games like Dark Souls and Elden Ring; in other words, not your typical Nintendo game. While The Duskbloods was originally scheduled to launch sometime this year, today the developer announced it's pushing the game's launch to 2027.

According to a post on The Duskbloods' X account, the main reason for the delay was balance-related. Here's the full statement:

While development of "The Duskbloods" is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027. We apologize to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support. During the network test, we saw active interest in the core concepts of the game, including combat, strategic depth, and player expression. To further enhance these aspects, we have decided to move the launch, allowing time for final adjustments to game rules and balancing.

We attended a hands-on preview session earlier this year and came away very positive, and sentiment was similar following the game's closed network test (that is, when the servers were working properly). It's not surprising that the devs have changes in mind following so much public feedback, though it is a little surprising that it will take until sometime next year for those adjustments to be complete.

#4265. GTA 6 Will Be Playable on XBOX One, According to Rockstar

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

A big part of what’s making the steadily-encroaching release of Grand Theft Auto 6 interesting in the current gaming climate, besides, y’know, being Grand Theft Auto 6, is that it’s only going to be available on consoles, and specifically XBOX and PlayStation family consoles. PC and Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 are being left out in the cold, at least for the time being, although rumors abound that the PC launch may come sooner than expected in order to beat out AI slop knockoffs.

I don’t claim to know all of the precise reasons for this particular launch strategy, beyond perhaps a pursuit for immediate at-launch optimization for the most readily-available consoles. That said, it would seem that, even if you own a particular console from the previous generation, you may still be able to play the game, albeit in a slightly diminished state.

Rockstar announced on its official news blog today that pre-loading for Grand Theft Auto 6 has officially begun, with the many who pre-ordered the game digitally now able to start downloading, and those who purchased codes-in-boxes able to start redeeming them and do the same. Buried within this announcement was a rather unexpected detail: it’ll be possible to play Grand Theft Auto 6 on the previous generation’s XBOX One console.

GTA 6, Rockstar's upcoming open-world adventure, is taking up 210 GB on PlayStation 5.

Here’s the interesting bit: since XBOX Cloud Gaming is also available on the XBOX One console, that means you can, in fact, play Grand Theft Auto 6 on an XBOX One by streaming it. At least as far as I’ve determined, the XBOX One will be the only previous-gen console that will be able to play this brand-new game, and an exceptionally high-end game at that.

Since XBOX Cloud Gaming is also available on the XBOX One console, that means you can, in fact, play Grand Theft Auto 6 on an XBOX One.

Of course, there are some catches here. First, no matter what XBOX console you’re playing on, any instance of Grand Theft Auto 6 played via Cloud Gaming will use XBOX Series S-tier graphical settings, i.e. not the best possible ones. Additionally, as is always the case with cloud streaming, how good the game looks and runs is largely dependent on the quality of your internet connection, so if you’ve got lousy speeds, this isn’t going to work well for you.

As GTA 6's launch approaches, everyone wants part of the PR pie, including internet ISPs.

On a semi-related note, Rockstar also confirmed that Grand Theft Auto 6 will work with Remote Play on both PlayStation and XBOX consoles, for those who want to stream the game from their console to elsewhere in their home.

I probably don’t need to remind anybody of this, but here it is anyway: Grand Theft Auto 6 is officially launching on Thursday, November 19, with the unlock time being whenever the clock strikes midnight in your particular time zone.

Whether through an installed digital copy or, apparently, on an XBOX One via Cloud Gaming, anyone who is interested in this game will, with certainty, be playing it as soon as it launches. I shudder to think what those poor digital storefronts are going to be going through at midnight on the 19th. Maybe wait until after school or work that day before you try to start playing, at least assuming you’re not one of the metric whoa-ton of people who are projected to be calling in sick that day.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is encroaching upon our reality, and upon its advent, there is a non-zero chance life will never be the same. If you’re not too busy playing the game for an indeterminate blur of time, maybe you can check out Rockstar’s official launch party in Miami the following weekend.

A massive music festival will be held in Miami the weekend following the game's release, with numerous big-name performers to participate.

#4264. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.
